news.title: MAGA News Channel Cuts Away as Interview Goes Off the Rails
news.text:
A right-wing channel abruptly cut away from an interview with a Donald Trump rallygoer after the segment quickly derailed.

During coverage of Trump’s rally in Youngstown, Ohio on Monday, Real America’s Voice cut to Bobby McNeily, a reporter for the Pro-Trump network. McNeily, who was inside the arena, introduced an interview with a man he spoke with earlier while he was waiting in line. The man was identified as Brian. 

McNeily opened by riffing on Brian’s Forrest Gump T-shirt, quoting the movie’s “I just felt like running” line and adding, “I love that movie.” Then the bit fell apart. 

Looking baffled, McNeily told viewers he was “hearing from friends” that the man beside him was “not a fan of President Trump.” 

“It’s very interesting,” McNeily said, “because I’ve never really spoken to anyone that I can recall, interviewing them, not a fan of President Trump, but standing in line to see him. Brian then revealed that it was his first Trump rally.

“What are you hoping to hear tonight?” McNeily asked. 

“What I hope to hear is not what I plan to hear… what I plan to hear is a bunch of rhetoric, a bunch of lies, a bunch of the same old script, that sort of stuff,” Brian said. 

“I’m here to get a firsthand perspective of the kind of lies and garbage and stuff that he’s going to probably be peddling for the next two years, as if the first two haven’t been bad enough.”

“Do you consider yourself a registered Democrat, or how would you vote before?” McNeily asked. 

“I was independent, because I consider myself moderate,” he said. 

“I was independent until JD Vance entered our ballot, and then I actually registered for a Republican. My strategy being, if I can keep him off the general election ballot by voting against him in a primary, then I get two chances to eliminate all these MAGA idiots. That’s my approach.” 

McNeily then followed up with a question about whether Vance’s selection had encouraged him.

“Oh, I can’t stand him,” Brian said. “I mean, it’s basically anybody that endorses or is endorsed by Donald is not a fan of mine.”

Moments later, the interview cut away from Brian mid-sentence. The network then cut back to a studio panel, including McNeily, who were asked for a “quick reaction.”

Host Grant Stinchfield marveled at how politely he thought Brian had been treated. 

“The left would not be as nice to us if we were at a, God forbid, Kamala Harris rally,” he said. “But he’s Trump-deranged, isn’t he?”

“Absolutely, Grant,” McNeily replied. Still, he said he was “holding out hope” for Brian. “I’m an optimistic guy.”

McNeily guessed that Brian had “listened to crazy far left outlets instead of actually really seeking the truth in all of this.”

The rally came three weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections. 

Trump was in Youngstown to campaign for Sen. Jon Husted, 59. The Republican was appointed to Vance’s old seat in 2025, after Vance became vice president. Husted is trailing former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown as the GOP fights to hold onto a state Trump won by double digits in 2024, according to the Hill. 

Trump’s swing through Ohio comes as his approval ratings hit historic lows. A Pew Research Center poll released last week found that only three in ten Americans now approve of the way Donald Trump is handling his job as president.

The Daily Beast has reached out to the White House and Real America’s Voice for comment.

RAVA right-wing channel abruptly cut away from an interview with a Donald Trump rallygoer after the segment quickly derailed.

During coverage of Trump’s rally in Youngstown, Ohio on Monday, Real America’s Voice cut to Bobby McNeily, a reporter for the Pro-Trump network. news.title: Trump repeatedly attacks Minnesota, Omar during Ohio campaign stop
news.text:
President Trump repeatedly brought up Minnesota and Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.) on Monday night while stumping for Republicans in Ohio ahead of the midterms.

Federal agents searched the home of Omar, a Somali-born American citizen, on Monday as part of a federal criminal investigation into Omar.

“Just look at what’s happening in the once great state of Minnesota. What a mess they have done,” Trump said in Youngstown. “And Ilhan, somebody was asking. I don’t know what they’re doing with it, but I can tell you this: she’s a disaster.”

He said Omar comes from “one of the worst countries anywhere on the planet.”

The crowd started chanting “deport” as he talked about Somalis in the U.S.

He brought up the massive pandemic-era fraud scheme that took place in Minnesota and involved some of the state’s Somali community. Hundreds of millions of dollars were stolen from a federally funded nutrition program.

“They came over here. They had nothing. They came from a government that doesn’t exist,” the president said. “They come from a part of the world that only knows how to kill each other.”

He accused Democrats in Minnesota of cheating in the elections, saying he thought he won the state in 2024 before “a rather large drop of votes” showed up. Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris won Minnesota in 2024.

“They cheat like hell. Aside from everything else, they cheat on the elections,” he said.

Earlier Monday Trump called Omar “totally crooked” after being asked about the federal agents searching her home.

“Well, I understand they’re looking at her very carefully,” he told reporters before departing the White House for Ohio. “I’ve always found her to be totally crooked personally, but that has nothing to do with me.”

“I think she’s a terrible person, but that’s really up to the DOJ,” he continued. “I have nothing to do with it.”

Last week, Trump said Minnesotans should “fight back” against the Somali immigrants in their state.

“The once Great State of Minnesota is being taken over by Somali Immigrants. There is Violence, Murder, and Mayhem all over the State,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. “The people of Minnesota must fight back.”

Minnesota has the largest population of Somalis in the U.S. and 1.07 percent, according to World Population Review. Most arrived as refugees, like Omar and her family, after a civil war in the country in the 90s.

news.title: Democrats have knives out for John Fetterman — but risk stabbing themselves
news.text:
“I’d love to see him as a Republican,” President Donald Trump told reporters Saturday.

He was speaking, of course, of Sen. John Fetterman, the maverick Pennsylvania Democrat who’s been increasingly willing to break with his party in recent months.

Trump’s comment revved up a rumor mill that Fetterman himself recently sought to tamp down.

“I don’t have a reason” to jump ship to the Republicans, he assured CBS’ Major Garret two weeks ago. 

Then he dropped a quiet bombshell. 

“If I’m 51” — that is, the Senate’s 51st Democrat and the deciding vote for the body’s control — “then I don’t know.” 

He continued the tease: “Let’s revisit after the midterms.” 

Fetterman has every reason to be coy — it makes him Washington’s most powerful kingmaker.

If he does switch parties, or becomes an independent caucusing with the GOP, the Democrats’ Election Day hill gets very steep: It means they’ll need a net pick-up of five seats to take the Senate — improbable given socialist-adjacent candidates in places like Maine, Texas, Michigan and elsewhere.

But more importantly, a Fetterman exit would be an ominous signal of coming attractions for his party. 

In 2024, the Democratic Party politburo lied about President Joe Biden’s fitness for a second term, then about Kamala Harris’ readiness for prime time. 

These Big Lies cost them the election, as I predicted then on these pages. 

In 2026, the Democrats’ Big Lie is about the Big Tent. 

That’s because the party’s tent is “big” only for the extremist left. 

If you want to “seize the means of production,” eliminate the Senate, the presidency and the Supreme Court, open the borders, defund the police, abolish prisons and deprive Israel of its right to self-defense, then top Democrats will lay down prostrate: You get a red-carpet welcome. 

But if you question the trans-right agenda, you risk excommunication by the party’s activist class and mutiny by your own staff, as Rep. Seth Moulton learned in 2024. 

If you want to close the borders, you’re a bigoted xenophobe.

If you don’t parrot Hamas’ lies about genocide, you’re a colonizer.

All grounds for excommunication, as Fetterman is finding out. 

Former President Barack Obama has swooned for Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed, a candidate who can’t condemn the Muslim Brotherhood and refuses to say that the Nazi leadership in Tehran “is a greater threat” than the multiracial democracy in Israel. 

New York Mayor Zoran Mandami blames Israeli Jews for the genocidal Oct. 7attack, while his wife boosts social posts celebrating that barbarism. 

A decade ago, Democrats would have had nothing to do with this fetishization of terrorists. Today they mainstream it. 

So where does that leave the likes of Fetterman — and the many Democrats like myself who fought for years for Democratic presidents and candidates? 

When Fetterman this year said how “liberating” it was “not to be a progressive” — after announcing his unwavering support for Israel in 2023 — the knives came out. 

His former staff members started a smear campaign; Rep. Brendan Boyle, a fellow Pennsylvania Democrat, called Fetterman “a disgrace.” 

Back in July, Fetterman set a condition for leaving the Democratic Party.

“If our party ever becomes . . . the anti-Israel party, you know, that’s when I would leave,” he told the Hill Nation Summit. “That’s been a moral clarity for me.” 

But half of House Democrats have already voted to cut off Israel aid — and with Democrats like New Jersey’s Adam Hamawy soon heading for Congress, the trend line is clear. 

If Fetterman does leave, the impact could be enormous.

He reflects the values of not just the anti-terror centrists, but of a broad swath of working-class voters who share his stances on immigration, gender, crime, race and so much else. 

That’s why his exit could start a trend. 

Fetterman already enjoys a 77% approval rating among Pennsylvania Republicans and 48% approval statewide.

In his home state, as in the rest of the country, nearly 7 in 10 voters identify as moderate or conservative, and they strongly reject the socialist revolution. 

So as the Democratic Jacobins try to guillotine him politically, they’ll only be executing themselves. 

Within the Democratic Party, the center has collapsed: 70% of voters think the party is out of touch with everyday voters, and nearly every poll finds their cultural and economic ideas far to the left of the median voter. 

Regardless of what happens on Nov. 3, that toxic brand bodes poorly for 2028 and beyond. 

The Pennsylvania maverick clearly senses that moderates are no longer welcome in his party.

If he bails out after November, the question will be how many of us he takes with him.

news.title: Report: Kamala Harris ‘Lays Groundwork’ for 2028 Campaign
news.text:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris is laying the groundwork for a third presidential campaign, speaking with major donors, hiring staff, and traveling to battleground states, according to a Wall Street Journal report.

The former vice president has told associates she remains undecided on another White House run, but she has taken steps that could precede a 2028 bid, the Journal reported, citing multiple people familiar with the conversations.

Harris has publicly tied her plans to the November midterms, telling a NAACP event in Michigan last month that the next cycle depends on this one.

“I have not decided if I’m going to run again,” Harris said, drawing a lengthy standing ovation. “I do sincerely believe ‘28 won’t matter if we don’t get through ‘26.”

The former Democrat nominee has appeared at a half-dozen private California fundraisers ahead of the midterms and joined a Democratic National Committee get-out-the-vote call urging more than 2,000 volunteers to knock on doors across a dozen states. She has also assembled a team of advisers, including chief of staff Candace Bond, a former ambassador to Trinidad and Tobago, and communications director Eduardo Negrón.

The Harris Victory Fund raised more than $10.3 million between January and September 2025, with $8.5 million of that coming from contributions under $200, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) filings.

Not everyone in her orbit is convinced. Some donors have told Harris directly that a bid would be a long shot, the Journal reported, and her husband, Doug Emhoff, has privately told people he would prefer she not run, though those close to him expect he would support a campaign.

The skepticism extends to her 2024 financial base. The Los Angeles Times contacted more than two dozen top donors to the largest pro-Harris super PAC in May, many of whom gave at least $1 million, and found little appetite for a repeat.

“I think it is too early to pick a favorite in the 2028 race, but Kamala Harris will not be my candidate,” one donor said.

Harris still leads most hypothetical 2028 Democrat primary polls and retains strong support among black voters. California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D), another potential contender, said in a September CNN interview he would not run if Harris entered, calling a two-Californian primary a “gift from God for everybody else.”

The possible bid comes after a 2024 cycle in which Harris secured the nomination without an open primary following President Joe Biden’s abrupt exit, then lost the Electoral College and popular vote to President Donald Trump. Harris first signaled her openness to another run in April, telling the Rev. Al Sharpton’s National Action Network convention she “might” enter the race.
news.summary:
Former Vice President Kamala Harris is laying the groundwork for a third presidential campaign, speaking with major donors, hiring staff, and traveling to battleground states.

news.title: Trump Teases Kansas Rally as Democrats Threaten 107-Year GOP Stronghold
news.text: President Donald Trump floated an upcoming rally to stump for Republican incumbent Senator Roger Marshall in Kansas as polling shows Democrat Adam Hamilton slightly ahead roughly three weeks from Election Day. Marshall, a doctor, is currently in the seat that has been held by the GOP since 1919, the longest ever for any party. In his post on Truth Social discussing the potential rally, Trump called him one of his "favorite Senators." Midterm elections are commonly viewed as a test of the political environment facing the party in power, and the president's party has historically lost seats during them. Republicans now hold a narrow majority in both the House and Senate. Trump carried Kansas by double digits over then-Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 election, underscoring the state’s Republican tilt. But Democrats have maintained a foothold in the state, with Laura Kelly in the governor’s mansion even as Republicans hold both U.S. Senate seats. When reached for comment about Trump's new post, Hamilton campaign spokesman Tyson Brody told Newsweek, "Washington is panicking over desperate, failing politician Roger Marshall. They’re sending in millions to try to distract from Marshall’s record of supporting the war in Iran, gutting healthcare, and raising prices on everything from gas to groceries. Marshall is turning to these desperate lies and false attacks because Kansans have learned Roger Marshall had pregnant mothers arrested and jailed over small medical debts, and voted to block the release of the Epstein files. Roger Marshall is desperate to hide from his record of protecting predators and preying on low-income families in Kansas.” Newsweek reached out to Marshall's campaign via email on Monday for comment. What To Know In his new post, Trump praised Marshall, calling him a wonderful person, who has been given a "bum rap" for allegedly requesting money owed to him by his patients. "If he didn’t make these requests, he would be breaking the Law, and subject to criminal liability and arrest," Trump added in his post. Earlier this month, election forecaster The Cook Political Report moved the race from Lean Republican to a Toss Up, adding to the potentially troubling signs for Republicans surrounding the contest. Cook said Hamilton is running an "increasingly strong race" while highlighting the attack ad against Marshall, an OB-GYN, over billing and collection practices at his office. Marshall had branded the ad targeting his practice a "lie." Meanwhile, Marshall has called Hamilton a "radical Democrat," adding that "his sermons are identical to the Democratic Party platform." Trump also threw jabs at Hamilton, saying that he loves high taxes, open borders and added that he wouldn't want the Democrat to be his pastor. Hamilton is pastor of the largest United Methodist Church in the country, the Church of the Resurrection. He founded the Kansas City-area congregation in 1990 at age 25, according to his campaign website. "He’s caused nothing but turmoil in his church, which has broken up, and is virtually at war with each other because of him. In his church, he has caused great anger and dissension, setting it back decades with discord and vitriol that will never be healed," Trump said in part in his post. He added that Hamilton is "not one of us" while touting his own support from evangelicals during the 2024 presidential election. In his lengthy post, the president accused Hamilton of mishandling allegations involving a church camp counselor whom Trump called a child predator. Hamilton's campaign has previously rejected those attacks and also told the Kansas Reflector in July that "there was no attempt at a cover-up" regarding the investigation into the counselor following reports of abuse beginning in 2005, the outlet says. “I can just say that our aim was to make sure that if we got anything wrong, we wanted to get it right,” Hamilton said to the outlet. "ROGER LOVES KANSAS, AND WILL NEVER LET YOU DOWN! I will be having a Kansas Style Rally, in Roger’s Honor, very soon. See you there!" Trump concluded in his post. What New Polling Reveals Recent polling shows Hamilton in the lead by a couple of points or a dead heat. Prediction market site Polymarket shows Marshall ahead with 63 percent versus Hamilton's 38 percent on Monday afternoon. A YouGov poll showed Hamilton with 48 percent of the potential vote compared to Marshall's 45 percent. One percent said someone else, 5 percent said undecided and 1 percent said they would not vote. The poll surveyed 2,255 likely voters in Kansas from September 24 to October 4 and had a 3.2 percent margin of error. A Trafalgar Group poll showed Hamilton had 44.4 percent of the potential vote compared to 43.5 percent for Marshall, 2 percent for Libertarian Party candidate David C Graham and 10.1 percent were undecided. The poll surveyed 1,095 likely voters across the state from September 29 to October 1 and had a margin of error of 2.9 percent. In a poll by The New York Times and Siena University last month, Marshall had 47 percent of the potential vote compared to 46 percent for Hamilton, and 7 percent of respondents said they did not know. The poll surveyed 605 likely voters from September 22 to September 30 and had a margin of error of 4.6 points. Marshall's 2020 Cookie Bill Over the weekend, Marshall took to X to highlight that his campaign paid an invoice dating back to 2020 involving a cookie vendor. "As some folks may have seen, there was a post on social media regarding an unpaid 2020 cookie bill. We have absolutely no idea how this happened, but rest assured as soon as it became known to us, we immediately attempted to contact the business in order to apologize, and we have repaid the bill from 2020, double," Marshall said. The post included a screenshot of the paid invoice to "Holly's Sweet Treats, LLC FOR $1,300." For more analysis from us on the numbers shaping U.S. politics and the 2026 midterms, sign up for Newsweek's Midterms Monitor newsletter. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Edward T. Cummins
news.summary: Senator Marshall is currently in the seat that has been held by the GOP since 1919, and polling shows Democrats could flip it.

news.title: Why I distrust current polls about the midterms
news.text:
We keep getting harassed by pollsters. 

They call our cellphones, text us and send emails begging us to participate. We do not.

In the age of AI, who knows where the information will go? We have no idea whether it is friend or foe doing the harvesting.

Many of our family and friends, mostly conservatives, feel the same. On the other hand, people of liberal bent are more likely to answer surveys, according to surveys. 

That’s why I don’t trust current polls about the midterms, which show the GOP behind in most contestable races. 

Is Texas really going to elect a blaspheming fake Christian like James Talarico to the U.S. Senate because Ken Paxton has a messy divorce? I don’t think so.

Eight years ago, the Democrats’ new blue hope at the time, the preppy Beto O’Rourke, lost to Sen. Ted Cruz, and Mr. Talarico makes Mr. O’Rourke look like Chuck Norris. 

Nor do I think that Michigan voters will send to the Senate a guy like Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, a Democrat who has campaigned with Hasan Piker, the f-bomb throwing anti-American Islamist/communist. 

Like Mr. Talarico, Mr. El-Sayed is bolting like a greyhound away from his leftist past. “Defund the police.” Who, me?

Much of the Democratic Party, like Mr. El-Sayed, supports a socialist takeover of the health care industry via “Medicare for all.” They assure us that the federal government will run it as efficiently as, say, the federal government, which is rife with fraud and waste and has racked up a $40 trillion national debt. 

Mr. El-Sayed was a big supporter of the climate hysteria scheme called the Green New Deal. His staff has been scrubbing online references to it since his primary opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens, rightly accused him of endangering Michigan’s auto industry. He beat her by less than 1 percentage point. 

Republicans in Michigan have a strong Senate candidate in Rep. Mike Rogers, who, among other things, has been outspoken against communist China’s espionage, cyber hacking, telecom security and Chinese investments in Michigan. 

He came within a whisker of winning the 2024 U.S. Senate race in Michigan, losing by less than 1 percent to Democrat Elissa Slotkin. 

On a more general level, the media are ignoring things like the upsurge in Republican voter registrations over the past decade. 

Announcing a voter registration initiative in January, Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin acknowledged, “Between 2020 and ’24 alone, our party lost a combined 2.1 million registered voters. Meanwhile, Republicans gained 2.4 million voters.”

In Pennsylvania, for instance, Democrats had a 916,000-voter advantage in 2016. But they now have an edge of only 206,000 in a state with 9 million registered voters. 

Nevada, in which Democrats were ahead, has swung back to a Republican advantage. In Florida, Republicans have increased their lead to more than 1.5 million registrations. 

In North Carolina, registered Republicans outnumber Democrats for the first time in 22 years, although independents account for the largest share of the electorate.

Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper is counting on name recognition and tagging his Senate opponent, Michael Whatley, as a Trump insider. Mr. Whatley chaired the North Carolina Republican Party and the Republican National Committee. Most polls show Mr. Cooper leading.

Mr. Whatley’s ads accuse Mr. Cooper of being soft on criminals and of being a career politician. So far, Mr. Whatley has not reminded voters about Mr. Cooper’s Achilles heel: his inexplicable embrace of the transgender agenda, which includes the medical mutilation of sexually confused children. 

In July 2023, Mr. Cooper vetoed three bills from the Republican-led legislature. One bars biological males from girls’ and women’s high school and college sports teams. Another bans medical sexual transitions for minors. A third restricts gender identity content in early grades and requires officials to inform parents about children’s pronoun changes.

With public support surging on these issues, legislators easily overrode Mr. Cooper’s vetoes and made them law. This suggests that adding a Trump-style “they/them” ad in North Carolina might prove effective. 

Meanwhile, day after day, the media keep unveiling polls that seem designed to discourage Republicans from voting. If there’s no hope, why bother?

But polls have been spectacularly wrong, and always against Republicans. In 1980, they had Ronald Reagan in a virtual tie with Jimmy Carter. Mr. Reagan won in a landslide, netting 489 electoral votes to Mr. Carter’s 49.

In 2024, polls showed Kamala Harris slightly favored to win nationally and in several battleground states. Donald Trump won the popular vote, all seven battleground states and took 312 electoral votes. 

Both parties need to motivate their base while convincing independents that they can be trusted to bring down gas prices, control crime, curb the cost of health care, keep the border secure, stand up to our enemies and resist—not abet—cultural rot. 

Democrats have no history of doing any of that. Quite the opposite.

In 2025, nine out of 10 Muslim voters went for Zohran Mamdani, a Democrat who is now New York City’s first Muslim/communist mayor. So did a third of the city’s Jewish voters, in a shocking display of suicidal empathy.

In Michigan, Mr. El-Sayed is counting on Muslims to vote heavily Democratic.

But if Christian voters outside Dearborn have even a slightly above average turnout, Mr. Rogers will win, no matter what the polls say. 

And that would be the case for Republicans nationally as well.

This column was first published at the Washington Times.

news.title: Musk spends $276M to help Republicans hold Congress
news.text:
NEW YORK >> Elon Musk has spent roughly $366 million in the 2026 U.S. midterm election cycle so far, $276 million of it since July to help Republicans retain control of Congress, even as Democrats’ chances of retaking the U.S. House and Senate have improved.

Musk’s largess, which was reported earlier by the New York Times, makes the world’s richest person likely the single-biggest political donor in this year’s races, according to campaign finance records.

There is a lot at stake for Musk, with Democrats in the U.S. House of Representatives calling for investigations into his government contracts as CEO of aerospace company SpaceX as well as his work running the Department of Government Efficiency under President Donald Trump.

Here is a breakdown of his political spending, which was confirmed by a spokesman for his super PAC, America PAC.

>> Musk has spent $366 million so far this election cycle, which began January 1, 2025.

>> At least $276 million so far has gone to Republican groups and his own super PAC since July. Of the $276 million in third-quarter donations:

>> $158 million went to the Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC set up to help elect Republicans to the Senate that is aligned with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, a Republican from South Dakota.

>> $20 million went to the Congressional Leadership Fund, the super PAC set up for House Republicans that is aligned with House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Louisiana Republican.

>> $76 million went to Musk’s America PAC.

>> $10 million went to the Lone Star Liberty PAC, which is supporting Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton’s run for the U.S. Senate in Texas, where recent polls have him in a dead heat against Democrat James Talarico.

>> $10 million went to the Republican Governors Association.

>> $2 million went to the Republican Attorneys General Association.

>> America PAC is helping Republican candidates in seven battleground states and nearly three dozen House races.

>> The new giving will be publicly disclosed when many super PACs are required to disclose their third-quarter spending on Thursday.

>> Musk has also donated more money through groups that do not disclose their donors, according to the New York Times report.

>> Roughly $90 million spent this cycle paid for work done in the prior election or supported other issues, including an unsuccessful candidate for the Wisconsin Supreme Court and a controversial program paying $1 million to registered voters who signed a petition supporting free speech and gun rights, according to an America PAC spokesman.

>> Musk spent roughly $290 million during the last election cycle in which Trump won the presidential election race against former Vice President Kamala Harris.
news.summary: NEW YORK >> Elon Musk has spent roughly $366 million in the 2026 U.S. midterm election cycle so far, $276 million of it since July to help Republicans retain control of Congress, even as Democrats’ chances of retaking the U.S. House and Senate have improved.

news.title: Talarico Takes on Biden's Border Policies and Data Centers in Texas Ads
news.text: Texas Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico is opening the week on offense with two new television ads, one in which he says he called out former President Joe Biden "for failing us on the border" and another going after Republican Ken Paxton over his ties to the data center industry. The spots land days after Talarico came back from a bout of flu that kept him off the campaign trail for more than a week, an absence Paxton and President Donald Trump seized on in recent days. He returned Friday with an unannounced appearance at the Austin City Limits music festival, his first public appearance since September 30. Taken together, the ads reflect the coalition Talarico needs to become the first Democrat to win statewide in Texas since 1994: Hispanic voters along the border who drifted toward Republicans during the Biden years, and rural and suburban voters fed up with data centers and their utility bills. Early voting starts in a week, and most polls have him narrowly ahead. Newsweek reached out to Talarico's campaign for comment on Monday. The Two Ads In the border spot, Talarico stands in front of a Texas flag and speaks directly to the camera. "I'll always put Texas before any political party," he says. "I called out Joe Biden for failing us on the border. I worked with Republicans to pass the largest property tax cut in Texas history." He has made the argument since July, when he unveiled a border plan in Terrell County and said Biden "and his administration failed us on our southern border." Republicans have questioned when that criticism began. Fox News Digital reported that his campaign could not point to a break with Biden while Biden was still in office, and Talarico has cited a speech from 2022. Republican strategist Mike Madrid told Newsweek in April that the centrist pitch was deliberate from the start. "His style and his appeal has been to be more centrist from the beginning," Madrid said. "In Texas, you can't do this with just Democrats. You've got to have Republicans." In the second ad, Talarico walks toward the camera as he makes the case against Paxton, the state's attorney general. "Ken Paxton is selling off Texas, our land, our water, our communities. Anything to make a buck," he says. "He gave data centers billions in special tax breaks and they gave him nearly half a million in campaign contributions." When the campaign posted the ad on X, it added a line of its own: "Data centers bankroll Paxton, they get tax breaks, and you get stuck with the bill." A note underneath said the ad "was made by humans, not AI," a reference to Paxton, whose campaign has aired spots built around an AI-generated Talarico. The contribution figure tracks with a NOTUS analysis of Federal Election Commission records, which found Paxton's campaign took in at least $448,000 through June from executives and committees tied to companies that build, run or invest in data centers. James Talarico Vs. Ken Paxton: Latest Polls Talarico has led most surveys since Paxton clinched the nomination, usually inside the margin of error. The RealClearPolitics average of polls taken from September 18 to October 8 has him at 48.1 percent to Paxton's 45.3 percent. The newest poll in that average, from the Republican-leaning Trafalgar Group, was fielded October 6 to 8, largely during Talarico's absence, and found him ahead 47 percent to 44 percent. YouGov and a New York Times/Siena College survey each had him up 6 points in early October, and a late-September Fox News poll put the gap at 2. "There is no evidence Texas voters are warming to the national Democratic message," Alex Patton, a Republican strategist with Ozean Media, told Newsweek earlier this year. "The data shows that Texas voters are responding to Talarico as a candidate and support for the opposition is softening." Paxton has polled better on the border. A Texas Pulse poll by the Texas A&M Bush School and ReconMR in late July found him ahead 48 percent to 44 percent on securing the U.S.-Mexico border. James Talarico Vs. Ken Paxton: Recent Developments in the Texas Race Talarico disclosed the flu on September 30, calling in by video to a U.S. Hispanic Business Council event in Edinburg he had planned to attend in person. "I guess I've been shaking too many hands on the campaign trail, and so I want to keep everybody safe," he said. Paxton's campaign responded by demanding "proof of life," setting up a "Tala-Freak-Out Tip Line" and circulating missing person posters, The Texas Tribune reported, while right-wing commentators promoted unverified theories about his absence. After a rally in San Antonio, Trump wrote on Truth Social that Talarico was "MISSING IN ACTION." Talarico, 37, has Type 1 diabetes, which the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says raises the risk of serious flu complications. "Hate to disappoint the conspiracy theorists, but James is still alive and meeting with voters at ACL today," spokesperson JT Ennis posted on X on Friday. The Money Game Talarico has raised more than Paxton in candidate fundraising, bringing in $27 million in the first quarter and $30 million in the second. Paxton's campaign said it raised more than $18 million from July through September, by far its best quarter. Talarico had not released his third-quarter numbers as of Monday. Outside spending has favored Paxton since September. Texas PAC, a super PAC affiliated with the Senate Leadership Fund, spent $131 million in 17 days, and Republican super PACs overall have steered more than $150 million toward Paxton, against roughly $4 million from Democratic super PACs for Talarico. AdImpact estimates total ad spending in the race has passed $440 million, the most of any Senate contest this cycle. Tesla CEO Elon Musk, the world's richest man, has also stepped into the race in his adopted home state, where he keeps a residence in Austin and built Starbase, the SpaceX company town in South Texas. Musk gave $10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, a group backing Paxton, along with $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, according to figures his representatives supplied to The New York Times this week. His own super PAC, America PAC, had spent more than $6 million by late September supporting Paxton and opposing Talarico, Federal Election Commission filings show. It is unclear how much the late money will move voters. "Can many millions of dollars poured in late to rough up Talarico allow Paxton to squeak through? We'll see," Calvin Jillson, a political scientist at Southern Methodist University, told Newsweek last week. Where James Talarico, Ken Paxton Stand on Data Centers Talarico has built part of his campaign around cracking down on data centers. His "Hold Data Centers Accountable Plan," released in July, would repeal the state's sales tax exemption for the industry, require developers to fund their own power and water infrastructure, mandate closed-loop water systems and give communities a say before projects break ground. He stopped short of the statewide moratorium some Texas Democrats have backed. He has pointed to an estimated $3.2 billion in state tax breaks for data center companies as money that could instead lower housing, child care and prescription drug costs. Paxton was slower to define a position. In a May appearance on the Valuetainment podcast, he called the issue "complicated" and said that on artificial intelligence the U.S. is competing with China and "we cannot lose that race." Governor Greg Abbott, who once declared Texas the "epicenter of AI development," has since moved to tighten oversight of new projects and end the industry's sales tax breaks. Paxton followed in August with his own "Texas First Data Center Plan." It backs Abbott's push to repeal tax incentives, would make data centers pay for the electricity infrastructure they need and use closed-loop cooling, and would restrict AI facilities in rural residential areas. Polling shows broad opposition to data centers in Texas. A University of Texas/Texas Politics Project poll in August found 57 percent of registered voters opposed building a data center in their community, 41 percent of them strongly, a result statistically unchanged from June. Nationally, the backlash has put pro-data center lawmakers in tossup races on the defensive, and voters in eight states are weighing data center ballot measures. Opposition runs highest in rural areas, where 62 percent opposed a local data center in the June survey, half of them strongly. Sixty percent of suburban voters also opposed it. Paxton's campaign has pointed to Lone Star Rising, the main pro-Talarico super PAC, which has taken about $10 million from LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman, a backer of data center growth. CBS Texas also found that Talarico voted for a data center sales tax incentive in 2023, though it never became law. James Talarico, Ken Paxton Stance on the Border Biden's name still carries weight along the border. Customs and Border Protection frequently logged more than 2 million migrant encounters a year during his presidency, and Democrats paid a price in 2024, when Trump flipped Hidalgo and Cameron counties and won Starr County by 16 points. It was the first time in a century Starr backed a Republican for president, according to the Associated Press. Talarico spent the summer trying to win those voters back. Asked on MS NOW whether Democrats had erred by neglecting border security, he answered, "Absolutely," and said, "National Democrats took the border for granted." An Emerson College poll in August found Hispanic voters breaking for him by 19 points, and a later survey for the Cook Political Report and TelevisaUnivision had him ahead 63 percent to 30 percent among Hispanic voters. Paxton, who sued the Biden administration scores of times as attorney general, has dismissed the shift. "James Talarico is a hypocrite who has taken a page out of the Joe Biden playbook," he said in a statement this summer. What Happens Next Talarico headlines a CNN town hall on October 14, his first big televised appearance since getting sick. Third-quarter fundraising reports are due to the Federal Election Commission the following day. Early voting runs October 19 to 30, and Election Day is November 3. Paxton has not yet accepted any of the four debate invitations Talarico has received. Democrats are treating the lead with caution. In interviews with Newsweek published Sunday, party strategists warned that narrow edges in Texas and other Senate races could vanish, pointing to 2024, when Kamala Harris's September lead was gone by November. "Every Democrat should be running as if they're 10 points behind," Doug Gordon, a Democratic strategist and co-founder of UpShift Strategies, told Newsweek. Patton, the Republican strategist, sees no sign of Democrats coasting. "You gotta run through the tape and leave nothing to chance," he said. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Samantha Beech and Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: Back from the flu, James Talarico hits Ken Paxton on data centers and breaks with Biden on the border in two new Texas Senate ads.

news.title: ‘I fell for it’: Trump’s fiercest blue-collar backers face a reality check
news.text:
Ohio residents who voted for Trump are now questioning whether he cares to deliver on his promises to revive the manufacturing industry and prioritize blue-collar jobs/work. Many who voted for him based on his proposed commitments to a thriving economy wonder where his priorities currently stand. 

Concerns are growing across the country with inflation in groceries, housing, and gas while the job opportunities and pay appear stagnant. One Ohio voter says Trump’s support of AI and data centers does not align with his previous commitments.

“I hate [AI and data centers] with a passion,” William Akel, a 26-year-old resident of Niles, Ohio, told The Washington Post. said. “AI is going to take the jobs, and then what jobs are we going to have? Probably fixing the AI?”

“I think he’s just lost in the sauce,” Akel added of Trump. “He sees [AI] as a way to make more money. … They’re putting billions and billions into all that. Where’s it all coming from? You’ve got people starving here.”

In Liberty, Ohio, Brian, a 54-year-old who voted for Trump in all three of his elections, echoed similar sentiments. “I’m extremely disappointed in him,” he said, preferring not to use his last name due to the heightened political landscape and out of fear to protect himself. “I fell for it.”

Trump remained committed when he visited Ohio earlier this month and spoke to a crowd at Butler High School in Vandalia, Ohio, telling potential voters it’ll be an economic boost to the area. “We want them,” Trump said. “Look, there’s so much money to be made for Ohio, you can’t just turn them off. They’ll go to China.”

Recently, a local nearby truck factory laid off nearly 1,400 workers, some of the same blue-collar workers Trump promised would have better opportunities under his administration. Kyle Bos, an employee with Navistar, the truck factory in question, told PBS he voted for Trump three times, but has lost faith in him.

"Something has to change politically in this country," said Bos, a member of the United Auto Workers who identifies as a centrist. "Seems like it just kept getting worse and worse and worse."

In 2024, over 3 million Ohio residents voted for Trump. That number may be significantly less as locals complain of continued rising costs for basic necessities. 

Akel admits he voted for Trump in 2020, chose Kamala Harris in 2024, and is undecided about the upcoming midterm elections. Brian says he now plans to vote only in local races in the upcoming election, saying he is not moved by either party’s candidates for Senate or governor. Like Akel, Brian is concerned about data centers. “We’re going to pay for all of this,” Brian said. “We always do.”

news.title: Elon Musk has spent $276 million on midterms to help Republicans retain control of Congress
news.text: Elon Musk has spent roughly $366 million in the 2026 US midterm election cycle so far, $276 million of ⁠it since July to help Republicans retain ⁠control of Congress, even as Democrats' chances of retaking the US House and Senate have improved. Musk's largess, which was reported earlier by the New York Times, makes the world's richest person likely the single-biggest political donor in this year's races, according to campaign finance records. There is a lot at stake for Musk with Democrats in the US House of Representatives calling for investigations into his government contracts as CEO of aerospace company SpaceX as well as his work running the Department of Government Efficiency under President Donald Trump. Musk has spent $366 million so far this election cycle, which began January 1, 2025. At least $276 million so far has gone to Republican groups and his own super PAC since July. Here is a breakdown of his political spending, which was confirmed by a spokesman for his super PAC America PAC. Of the $276 million in third-quarter donations: * $158 million went to the Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC set up to help elect Republicans to the Senate that is aligned ⁠with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, a Republican from South Dakota. * $20 million went to the Congressional Leadership Fund, the super PAC set up for House Republicans that is aligned with House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Louisiana Republican. * $76 million went to Musk's America PAC. * $10 million went to the Lone Star Liberty PAC, which is supporting Republican state Attorney General Ken Paxton's run for ⁠the US Senate in Texas, where recent polls have him in a dead heat against Democrat James Talarico. * $10 million went to the Republican Governors Association. * $2 million went to the Republican Attorneys General Association. America PAC is helping Republican candidates in seven battleground states and nearly three dozen House races. The new giving will be publicly disclosed when many super PACs are required to disclose their ⁠third-quarter spending on Thursday. Musk has also donated more money through groups that do not disclose their donors, according to the New York Times report. Roughly $90 million spent this cycle paid for work done in the prior election or supported other issues, including an unsuccessful candidate for the Wisconsin Supreme Court and a controversial program paying $1 million to registered voters who signed a petition supporting free speech and gun rights, according to an America PAC spokesman. Musk spent roughly $290 million during the last election cycle in which Trump won the presidential election race against former Vice President Kamala Harris.
news.summary: There is a lot at stake for Musk with Democrats in the House of Representatives calling for investigations into his government contracts as CEO of SpaceX as well as his work running the Department of Government Efficiency under President Donald Trump

news.title: New 2028 presidential poll shows 2 potential frontrunners
news.text:
As buzz around potential 2028 presidential candidates grows, a new poll shows clear frontrunners in hypothetical Democratic and Republican primaries.

In a new Focaldata/Financial Times poll released Sunday, Oct. 11, it was a battle of the VPs: Former Vice President Kamala Harris and current Vice President JD Vance both led their respective party’s potential primary.

According to the survey, Harris leads among Democrats with 30% support, followed by California Gov. Gavin Newsom at 15% and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg tied at 9%.

On the other side of the aisle, Vance leads with 38% of Republicans, followed by Secretary of State Marco Rubio at 24%, with Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis receiving 9% of support from GOP respondents.

The poll surveyed 2,553 U.S. adults from Oct. 2 to Oct. 5, according to Focaldata.

Is anyone running for president?

No, but many have started to signal their potential bids in recent weeks.

In September, Newsom told CNN he would not run in 2028 if Harris decided to campaign for the Democratic presidential nomination again. In a podcast appearance in August, Buttigieg said he was “more inclined than not” to make another run for the White House.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Maryland, said he was “kicking the tires” at a potential run in 2028 in an appearance on NBC’s "Meet the Press" in August.

More: Kamala Harris, Ocasio-Cortez and the rocky midterms campaign trail

On the Republican side, Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas has fueled speculation about another White House bid.

"It’s no secret that I want to be president," Cruz said in August on Texas Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick’s podcast.

Others, like Rubio, haven't been so direct.

"I don't know what the future holds, but I have no plans at this time," Rubio said during an official visit to Colombia in September. "I'm not a candidate for anything right now. And I’m 100% focused on my job."

Fernando Cervantes Jr. is a trending news reporter for USA TODAY. Reach him at fernando.cervantes@usatodayco.com and follow him on X @fern_cerv_.

news.title: Kamala Harris Unveils Ambitious Social Security and Medicare Plans – What It Means for You
news.text:
Vice President Kamala Harris has recently revealed her comprehensive proposals aimed at strengthening Social Security and Medicare, two critical programs impacting the financial well-being of millions of Americans. Here’s a breakdown of her visionary plans and how they could affect your finances.

Harris is determined to increase Social Security benefits, especially for low-income retirees, to alleviate the financial strain of basic necessities. She also plans to adjust the payroll tax cap, suggesting that higher earners contribute more to ensure the program’s sustainability.

Acknowledging the invaluable work of caregivers, Harris proposes Social Security credits for individuals leaving the workforce to care for family members, ensuring they are not penalized financially for their service.

In terms of Medicare, Harris advocates for lowering the eligibility age to 60, expanding coverage to include dental, vision, and hearing services, and negotiating drug prices to reduce healthcare costs for seniors.

By implementing these policies, Harris aims to enhance financial security for seniors and future retirees by increasing benefits, raising payroll taxes for high earners, providing earlier access to Medicare, and expanding Medicare coverage to reduce out-of-pocket expenses.

While her proposals have garnered support from progressives and advocacy groups, they also face opposition due to concerns about costs and government involvement in healthcare. Nevertheless, Harris’ vision for the future of Social Security and Medicare promises greater security and peace of mind for millions of Americans. With the 2024 election approaching, these issues are set to shape political discourse and have profound effects on individual finances and the economy.

news.title: Which Portland? GOP ad buyer chooses wrong state for Senate campaign
news.text:
A Republican group supporting Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, accidentally ran ads targeting her Democratic Senate opponent Troy Jackson in Portland, Oregon – not Portland, Maine.

The media vendor for Defending Main Street, a Republican Super PAC, spent about $25,000 on digital advertising in the wrong state, a spokesperson from Defending Main Street confirmed.

“The error was identified, the ads were immediately stopped and corrected, and the vendor is refunding Defending Main Street the full amount of the misplaced spend,” the spokesperson continued. “No donor funds will be lost as a result of the vendor’s error.”

Cross Screen Media, the ad buyer that reportedly made the mistake, took "100%" responsibility, according to the 1903 Group, who handled the ad buying. They confirmed that they stopped the wrong campaign, got the ads up to the right area and refunded the spend.

The race between Collins and Jackson is one of the most competitive in the country. Collins is the only Republican senator to represent a state won by former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election, and Democrats see defeating her as crucial to flipping Congress, which is currently narrowly controlled by Republicans, 53-47.
news.author: Usa Today

news.title: Dem’s spouse doesn’t want them to run for president in 2028. And donors agree
news.text:
The husband of former Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris doesn’t want his wife to run for president again.

The Wall Street Journal is reporting that former Second Gentleman Doug Emhoff has privately told people that he would prefer that his wife stay out of the 2028 White House race.

But people close to Emhoff said that they expect that he would be supportive if Harris were to take the presidential plunge again.

The nj.com logo
A subscription is required to read this story.

Subscribe now to continue.

Harris lost the 2024 race to Republican Donald Trump after her boss, former President Joe Biden, withdrew from the race.

Harris is looking at running again, even though she lost the popular vote and the tally in the Electoral College to Trump.

And it’s not just Emhoff who has his doubts.

Donors have reportedly told Harris directly that another White House campaign would be “a long shot.”

Perhaps laying the groundwork for another run, Harris has attended a number of Democratic fundraising events and has campaigned for candidates running in this year’s midterm elections.

Harris last week got on a call with the Democratic National Committee and more than 2,000 volunteers, urging them to help with get-out-the-vote efforts in a dozen states, according to the New York Post.

“I have not decided if I’m going to run again,” she said at an NAACP event in Michigan last month. “I do sincerely believe ’28 won’t matter if we don’t get through ’26.”

Some Harris allies who have known and worked with the former vice president are “skeptical” she’ll run for president again, the Post said.

Harris’ fellow Californian, Gov. Gavin Newsom, has said that he would not run in 2028 if Harris does.

news.title: We’ve tracked $80M of spending on almost 170 AI‑generated political ads this year — it’s weird
news.text:
We are researchers who have been studying political advertising through the Wesleyan Media Project since 2010. This election cycle – using data from media reports, student coders and AdImpact, a firm that tracks political ad spending – we’ve tracked about US$80 million in spending on almost 170 unique ads that use AI.

What we found has surprised us: AI use spans from hyperrealistic deepfakes to subtle enhancements; Republican sponsors – both candidates and interest groups – are much more likely to use AI than are Democratic sponsors; and, thanks to a patchwork of state legislation, many of these ads do not disclose the use of AI at all.

From deepfakes to subtle edits

An assortment of politicians and watchdog groups have expressed concern about campaigns using generative AI to produce deepfakes – synthetic videos showing people doing things they did not do – that might deceive voters.

We’ve noticed several ads containing hyperrealistic deepfakes of famous politicians, including Donald Trump, Nancy Pelosi, Barack Obama, Kamala Harris and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. Ocasio-Cortez, in particular, is a favorite among Republican advertisers, appearing in at least five ads.

We’ve seen deepfakes in which a Republican Senate candidate from Louisiana drives a school bus full of undocumented immigrants, a Republican candidate for governor from South Carolina walks arm in arm with drag queens, and an ad in which Liz Cheney, Mitt Romney and Mike Pence are seen carrying pitchforks on the White House lawn.

Related: Minnesota passes the nation’s first ban on ‘nudification’ apps

People who are not politicians made appearances, too, including a fake Dr. Anthony Fauci, seen running around a state fair with a huge syringe, presumably eager to vaccinate everyone. We’ve also noticed several ads in which AI was used to generate crowds or constituents.

In several cases, AI was used to enhance visuals rather than generate something new. One ad from Chip Keating, a Republican candidate for governor in Oklahoma, includes an AI disclaimer, but it doesn’t specify exactly how AI was used. Ads that use AI to enhance visuals don’t necessarily look different from ads that were created in the pre-AI era, which makes it difficult for viewers to discern whether they depict something false.

A partisan gap

Republicans – both candidates and groups such as super PACs and 501(c) organizations – are much more likely to use AI in their ads than are Democrats, according to our research.

In fact, Republican candidates or pro-Republican groups were behind 80% of the ads we tracked and 83% of the spending.

We can only speculate as to why Republicans dominate the use of AI in political advertising in 2026. In general, Democrats tend to take on a regulatory mindset when it comes to political campaigns, favoring limits on campaign spending and required disclosures. In 2022, for instance, only Senate Democrats and two independents voted to advance the DISCLOSE Act that would have required additional campaign finance disclosures for super PACs, labor unions and corporations. Republicans, by contrast, tend to be more in favor of a free market approach.

These more general philosophies may be reflected in the parties’ use of generative AI for political advertising, something about which voters are worried. Polling shows broad support for more regulation, with 78% of registered voters favoring a ban on AI content that makes deceptive claims about candidates.

Disclaimers all over the map

Because regulation of AI in advertising depends on a patchwork of state legislation, many of these ads are not required to disclose the use of AI. This lack of disclaimers makes tracking AI use in ads challenging. Our team has relied on media coverage and trained student coders to flag ads that are potentially AI-generated.

Across 35 states, only 31% of the ads we tracked – representing 22% of the spending – disclosed the use of AI tools. The wording of these disclaimers was all over the map. For example, one Georgia ad included the disclaimer, “This video has been manipulated or generated with artificial intelligence,” while an Oklahoma ad said, “Political satire. AI-generated images do not depict actual events.” A North Carolina state Senate ad said, “You guessed it! AI was definitely used to generate these silly video clips.”

Laws don’t drive disclosure

Some advertisers voluntarily disclose the use of AI even when they are not required to do so. Sometimes, the opposite occurs – advertisers don’t include disclaimers even when state law requires them to. In fact, we’ve found that a state law that requires disclaimers on ads that use AI has very little relationship with the actual use of disclaimers.

In states without laws governing the use of AI in political ads, 32% of ads contained a disclaimer; by contrast, in states with laws governing the use of AI, 29% contained a disclaimer. This comparison, however, is not perfect, as some of the ads in our database aren’t covered by their state’s law. Some states, such as Colorado, have laws that apply only to candidate deepfakes and thus exclude other uses of AI. In other instances, such as in Louisiana, an AI law was enacted after the ad aired.

Community Voices: Political debates matter if we treat them as more than theater

Minnesota law generally bans deepfakes in political ads, but an ad featuring synthetic video of Democratic Senate candidate Peggy Flanagan aired in May 2026 anyway. Whether it violated state law is uncertain, as the law requires that the media be “so realistic that a reasonable person would believe it depicts speech or conduct of an individual who did not in fact engage in such speech or conduct.”

Moving forward, the real policy challenge will revolve around transparency, the enforceability of existing laws and simply figuring out what type of disclosure would be helpful to voters.

Travis N. Ridout, Professor of Government and Public Policy, Washington State University; Erika Franklin Fowler, Professor of Government, Wesleyan University, and Michael Franz, Professor of Government, Bowdoin College

The 2026 U.S. midterm campaigns are the first in which AI-generated political ads are regularly appearing on people’s televisions and social media feeds.

news.title: Ohio Early Voting Data is Stark Warning for Jon Husted
news.text: Early voting data from Ohio could be a stark warning for GOP candidate and incumbent Republican Senator Jon Husted. Husted faces a challenge from former Senator Sherrod Brown in a special election to finish the term for which Vice President JD Vance was elected in 2022. With the campaign season in its final weeks, a new CNN analysis shows that after the first few days of early voting, affiliated Democrats make up larger shares of pre-election voters than in the 2024 presidential election. Even in Republican parts of the state. Historically, the party in the White House loses seats in the midterms when the president is unpopular. All 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are up for election in November, along with key gubernatorial races. Democrats need 17 seats to win the Senate, while Republicans need 20. Republicans currently hold a slim majority in the House, 219 to 213, and need 218 seats to take control. The midterms could alter the course of Trump’s presidency and reshape how the administration proceeds with its legislative priorities if Republicans lose their majority in either chamber. What To Know About Early Voting Data In 2024, by this time, Republicans led Democrats by 30 percentage points in counties that voted for President Donald Trump by 20 points or more, according to CNN, which cited data from the Ohio Secretary of State. Now, that gap has shrunk to only 5 points. In other counties, voters have also shifted. Counties that voted most strongly for former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024 are now about 25 points more Democratic, CNN reports. The data could signal a positive environment for Democrats and a warning sign for the GOP, with the midterm elections now only weeks away. However, it is still early, and Ohio is only at about 11 percent of its total early voting turnout from 2022, per CNN. Early voting does not predict voting outcomes or intentions, and you cannot extrapolate a candidate from early eagerness to head to the polls. Newsweek emailed the Brown and Husted campaigns for comment. Recent polls show a continued downward slide in Trump’s national approval, which has, in turn, fueled Democratic hopes of winning back voters. Sherrod Brown vs. Jon Husted: What The Latest Polls Say The latest polls show a tight race, with Brown leading. The current RealClearPolitics average puts Brown 3.1 points ahead at 47.3 to Husted’s 44.2. CNN had Brown six points ahead, 49 to 43, while YouGov had Brown four points ahead, 49 to 45. Other polls showed slimmer averages: Quantus Insights put Brown one point ahead, 48 to 47, while co/efficient had Husted leading by a point, 46 to 45. Prediction markets paint a different picture. On both Polymarket and Kalshi, Brown leads, but the race is far less close than the polls currently show. Polymarket puts Brown at 62 percent to Husted’s 40 percent, while Kalshi has Brown at 60 percent to Husted’s 40 percent. The Latest Developments in the Ohio Senate Race Husted and Brown continue their campaigns and have shared multiple social media posts as they appeal to Ohioans and push their policy priorities. On Sunday, October 11, Husted shared a link to a Spectrum News article and wrote: “Whether it’s lowering energy costs, requiring simple photo ID to vote, or banning Members of Congress from trading stocks, Democrats voted NO—thwarting the will of the American people.” He then shared a message wishing a Happy Columbus Day, writing “In 1492, Christopher Columbus set sail and discovered land that would become the greatest nation in the world,” and encouraging people to “Have a safe and fun long weekend with family and friends.” Meanwhile, Brown shared a picture of himself at a campaign event where he wrote, “Hardworking folks in Youngstown know the system is rigged and they’re ready to fight back. That’s why, in 23 days, we’re going to win.” He then shared a post that directly referenced the war in Iran. “I’ll vote to end the war the first chance I get,” Brown wrote. Husted has previously called for the conflict to end quickly while continuing to oppose Democratic efforts to restrict the administration’s military authority. Why The Ohio Senate Election Matters in the 2026 Midterms Ohio could help to determine control of the Senate and has become one of the most closely watched states of the 2026 midterms. Both the Senate and gubernatorial races are hanging close. Back in 2024, Trump won Ohio by 11 points and carried it by 8 points in 2016 and 2020, respectively. But the Buckeye State backed former President Barack Obama in 2008 and 2012. And the economy could be pivotal for voters in the midterms and, in turn, turn the state into a competitive ground once again. Forty-nine percent of Ohio voters view the economy as their top issue, and 76 percent believe Trump’s policies have increased the cost of living, as per polling from CNN. Discontent over the war in Iran could also be key for voters, as concerns over affordability continue and the conflict drives high gas prices in the state. news.title: Trump shares fake Denzel Washington endorsement that was debunked days earlier
news.text:
President Donald Trump posted a fabricated quote attributed to Denzel Washington on his Truth Social account Monday, spreading a fake endorsement that fact-checkers had publicly debunked two days earlier.

The image Trump posted was a screenshot from an X account called Red Eagle Updates. Under the word “BOOM,” it showed Washington’s photo alongside the supposed quote: “I’ve worked with a lot of people in my life, and I’ve never met anyone braver, smarter, or who cares more about America than Donald Trump. He’s a great friend and an even better president. I’m proud to be a steadfast supporter, and I’ll never apologize for it.” The original post then asked readers, “Do you agree with Denzel? YES or NO?”

The problem: Washington never said it.

Snopes rated the quote an “incorrect attribution” over the weekend, noting it had circulated for at least several months and that searches of major outlets, including Fox News and Newsmax, turned up no reporting that Washington had ever praised Trump. The same words have previously been pinned on Matthew McConaughey and Mick Jagger.

The Red Eagle Updates post, published Saturday evening, had drawn about 214,900 views before Trump shared it to his own following without comment early Monday.

To boot, Washington’s political donations points the other way. 

Federal Election Commission records show he gave $28,500 to Barack Obama’s 2008 campaign and $27,000 to Hillary Clinton’s 2016 run against Trump, Newsweek reported. Newsweek also noted that just before the fake quote, Trump’s account shared a post boasting that he “DANCED off the stage in Tennessee” and that “Democrats want you think he’s losing it.”

Fake Washington endorsements of Trump date back nearly a decade.

PolitiFact rated one “Pants on Fire” in November 2016, and FactCheck.org debunked another in 2021, when Washington’s representative called it “a complete fabrication.” Snopes noted that such hoaxes often borrow the names of actors known for tough-guy roles, like Clint Eastwood, Tom Selleck and Sam Elliott, to make them more believable.

Washington has kept his votes to himself. Asked at a December 2016 screening of his film “Fences” whom he had supported, he told reporters, “None of your business.”

Trump’s account has shared false endorsements before. 

In 2024, it posted a claim that JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon had endorsed him, which the bank quickly denied. That August, Trump shared AI-generated images suggesting Taylor Swift and her fans backed him, including one of Swift as Uncle Sam urging people to vote for him, captioned “I accept!” Swift later cited those images when she endorsed Kamala Harris.

news.title: The Senate races most likely to flip less than a month from Election Day
news.text:
(The Hill) — The race for control of the Senate is heating up, with forecasters increasingly moving races in the Democrats’ direction less than a month out from the election.

Last week, nonpartisan election forecasters Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball from the University of Virginia Center for Politics shifted Senate races in Kansas, New Hampshire, North Carolina, Alaska and South Carolina in Democrats’ favor.

President Donald Trump’s tanking approval ratings and high costs associated with the war in Iran and the tariff war with Canada are making it difficult for Republicans to navigate the persistent headwinds, though some candidates have broken with the president on certain issues as they differentiate themselves from the White House and national party.

And while Democrats see a favorable political environment, it’s not guaranteed that it will be enough to push them into majority-making territory.

Here’s a look at the Senate races most likely to flip less than one month out:

The Tar Heel State has often served as Democrats’ metaphorical “Lucy and the football,” disappointing the party time and again at the presidential and Senate level, though they’ve fared better in gubernatorial races.

But the party notched a strong recruit in former Gov. Roy Cooper (D), with recent polling showing him leading former Republican National Committee (RNC) chair Michael Whatley anywhere from single to double digits.

The Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC aligned with Senate GOP leadership, has pulled money from the race; the Senate Majority PAC, the super PAC aligned with Senate Democratic leadership has as well, though to a lesser extent. However, that doesn’t mean either group has withdrawn entirely from the race financially.

The Last Frontier has also served as an unexpected bright spot for Democrats thanks to another strong recruit in former Rep. Mary Peltola (D).

The state is generally reliably Republican, with Trump winning the state by 13 points in 2024. However, Sabato’s Crystal Ball felt encouraged to move it into the “lean Democrat” category — Cook Political Report rates it as a “toss up” — given several recent surveys from strong pollsters.

Another notable sign is the fact that Vice President JD Vance has campaigned in the Last Frontier, while the president is expected to be there this week. Still, Miles Coleman and Kyle Kondik of Sabato’s Crystal Ball wrote on Tuesday in an analysis that Sullivan is a tough incumbent to beat.

“Though Alaska is, demographically, one of the youngest states, both the AARP poll and the more recent NYT poll show Sullivan carrying voters older than 45,” they wrote. “A couple of other pollsters have also shown a closer race: a late September poll from Quantus Insights had the race tied, while a couple of other conservative pollsters had Sullivan narrowly leading.”

Peltola also came under scrutiny after The New York Times reported last month about the former congresswoman’s allegedly abusive behavior towards staff — accusations her campaign has denied while noting that she has “sometimes struggled to deal with her grief” from losing her husband and mother. It’s unclear from polling if that’s hurt her Senate bid against Sullivan.

Like many of the competitive Senate races being closely watched next month, the Ohio Senate is regularly polling within the margin of error. Sen. Jon Husted (R) is running in a special election to fill the remainder of Vance’s seat in the Senate against former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D), one of the rare Democrats who has won statewide in the Buckeye State.

Ohio has trended away from Democrats in recent cycles, so much so that it wasn’t even considered one of the six swing states during the 2024 presidential election. And Brown’s loss to Sen. Bernie Moreno (R) that same cycle was another indicator of Ohio’s rightward shift.

As some news outlets like the Times have noted, some voters still think Brown is the sitting senator while Husted is lesser known to voters. If Ohio swings back toward Democrats next month, it would offer one of the first real signs that Democrats could be in for a very good night — and that they may be able to reverse some of their losses moving into the next election cycle.

Democrats have long tried to oust Sen. Susan Collins (R) in past elections, but the GOP senator has proved a formidable candidate and is the only Senate Republican to represent a state former Vice President Kamala Harris won in 2024.

Former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson (D) replaced populist Graham Platner as Democrats’ nominee to take on Collins in the Pine Tree State after numerous scandals forced Platner out of the race.

Jackson and Democrats broadly have sought to hit Collins specifically over her vote to confirm Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who was among the majority in ruling to overturn Roe v. Wade in 2022. The issue is nuanced for the GOP senator who supports access to abortion and has supported legislation aimed at codifying federal abortion access.

Democrats have also hit Collins over a recent ProPublica investigation, which alleged that GOP senator was involved in a pay-to-play scheme aiming at garnering contributions in exchange for government contracts to the defense contractor Navatek. Collins and her campaign have vehemently denied the allegations, calling it a “partisan hit” and “offensive” and pointing out that the allegations came from a convicted felon.

It’s unclear how much the controversy will electorally impact Collins as polling in the race shows a tight contest, and the GOP senator has proved she can win in tough races.

Michigan is seen as one of Republicans’ best pickup opportunities this cycle with Sen. Gary Peters (D) retiring. Former Rep. Mike Rogers (R) narrowly lost to Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D) in 2024, making him a formidable recruit in the 2026 cycle.

Republicans were eager to have former Wayne County health director Abdul El-Sayed as their Democratic opponent instead of the more centrist Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), seeing him as too far left for the swing state.

Yet, Rogers has increasingly staked positions breaking with the Trump administration, such as calling for the war in Iran to end and calling for the tariff war with Canada to be over. He’s not the only Senate Republican candidate to do that this cycle, though the fact that he’s called on Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to make a deal with Canada underscores the urgency many GOP challengers are feeling to turn things around before next month.

The Lone Star State has been another figurative “Lucy and the football” for Democrats after former Rep. Beto O’Rourke (D) narrowly lost to Sen. Ted Cruz (R) in 2018, later losing by a wider margin against Gov. Greg Abbott (R) in the 2022 governor’s race.

Trump’s travel to Texas — including his quips calling Republican Ken Paxton a “little controversial” and a “pain in the a–” — coupled with different leaked audio clips of Paxton trickling out last week have shown an increasingly volatile race. The president has even encouraged Paxton to debate Democrat James Talarico.

At the same time, Republicans have a clear edge in spending in Texas, which is expensive state given its multiple media markets. The ad-tracking firm AdImpact reported on Friday that Republicans had spent more than $51 million alone in future ad buys in the state compared to Democrats, who had committed nearly $5 million.

If Democrats flip the Iowa Senate seat in November, it likely indicates there’ll be a wave election. Handicapper Inside Elections rates the race as a “tilt Republican,” though Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball have moved it slightly further toward the Democrats and have called it a “toss up” in recent months.

Republicans have a strong recruit in Rep. Ashley Hinson (R), and the Hawkeye State hasn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate since former Sen. Tom Harkin’s (D) reelection in 2008. The state went for Trump by 13 points in 2024. Recent polling also has Hinson narrowly leading.

But forecasters have noted that the price of fertilizer and gas are concerns in the state, and Hinson has also gone so far as to call for Trump to end the war in Iran. AdImpact also noted that Iowa Democrats have narrowly hold an edge there in future ad reservations — only one of eight competitive Senate races where that’s the case.

The Sunflower State’s Senate race turned into an unexpected marquee contest this cycle, with Democrat Adam Hamilton notching several high-profile endorsements, including from two former Republican governors. Kansas hasn’t elected a Democrat since 1932, meaning Hamilton faces steep odds in toppling Sen. Roger Marshall (R).

Marshall has received scrutiny more recently over his handling of taxpayer funds and for suing hundreds of patients over medical debt, while Hamilton has received scrutiny over his handling of a child sex abuse scandal at his church.

An attorney for Marshall told MS NOW and the Kansas Reflector that the official office and campaign side both comply with campaign finance rules and Senate ethics rules. Rogers has also defended his decision to sue medical patients, saying he acted appropriately.

Hamilton told the Kansas Reflector he would have handled the initial reports of abuse, which were ultimately reported to officials, differently but also said that “there was no attempt at a cover-up” during the church’s investigation.

“Kansas has not elected a Democratic senator since 1932, and we’d still be surprised if that streak ends this year,” Kondik of Sabato’s Crystal Ball wrote last month, while noting they were shifting the race slightly toward Democrats.

The Granite State serves as Republicans’ second-best pickup opportunity should they have a better-than-expected Election Day. The GOP notched a strong recruit in former Sen. John E. Sununu, whose last name is a political dynasty in the state, and he’ll be running on the same ballot as Gov. Kelly Ayotte (R), who’s expected to win reelection next month.

But Cook Political Report’s Jessica Taylor suggested Trump’s underwater approval ratings in the state, current polling on the race and an expectation that Sununu could underperform Ayotte given how voters weigh federal and statewide races make Pappas the favorite right now.

“This race could still end up being closer than it should be given the national environment,” Taylor wrote. “Democratic ads hitting Sununu for his own work for a lobbying firm seem to have penetrated, but Pappas — who weathered a barrage of attack ads over the summer for his now-husband’s lobbying work for Amazon — also has work to do in the closing weeks to rally voters who aren’t fans of the Democratic Party either.”

The Senate races in Minnesota, South Carolina, Nebraska and Georgia are also being closely watched by both parties as the races take the temperature of electorates in more Democratic- and Republican-leaning states.

None of these states are expected to flip in November given their more partisan leanings, though upsets in any of these races would offer a telltale sign of a good night for one of the parties or another sleeper race observers missed.
