news.title: The Media, the Midterms, and the Fine Print
news.text:
We've seen this movie before.

In 2024, it was easy to see how polls were artificially boosting Kamala Harris. The crosstabs told us that President Donald Trump was making huge gains with black voters, yet the top lines were claiming that Kamala was somehow running ahead at the same time.

I wasn’t then, and still am not, a pollster or expert, but even I knew the math didn’t add up. It wasn’t a feeling or wishful thinking. The numbers just didn’t make sense. Lo and behold, I was right.

Is something similar happening this year? It could be, and the same outlets that spent months forecasting a Republican wipeout have started hedging.

According to a report from the Daily Signal, The New York Times, The Washington Post, and Newsweek have all run pieces in recent days conceding that the picture is less lopsided than advertised, under headlines like "Democratic Optimism in Six Senate Races May Be a Mirage," "3 Bright Spots for the G.O.P.," and "How Much Can Republicans Outrun Trump's Approval?"

Newsweek even dampened Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer’s (D-N.Y.) optimism. After listing Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, Ohio, and Texas as states where Democrats appear to hold a polling edge, the outlet added a rather significant caveat.

"But Republicans have outperformed polling averages in many of those same states over the past few elections," Newsweek reported. "Polling errors are not necessarily repeated from cycle to cycle. But a similar pro-Republican polling error this cycle would not bode well for Democrats' chances of flipping the Senate."

That caveat is quite important. Republicans have beaten their poll numbers in recent presidential and midterm elections, and most experts estimate conservatives underpoll by three to five points, which is enough to swing any close race.

ICYMI: No, Just No: Sen. Chuck Grassley, 93, Files for Reelection

The Times found even more for Democrats to worry about.

Ruth Igielnik wrote late last month that GOP Senate candidates are outrunning Trump's popularity in their states, "sometimes by double digits," and winning over some voters who say they want Democrats to control the chamber. The paper's polling also found that 70% of Republicans consider their party united, while Democrats split roughly in half on the same question about their own. Then there's Rasmussen Reports, which on Monday showed Hispanic voters favoring Republicans 50% to 42%. So much for the claim that Hispanics are abandoning the GOP. Right?

The same survey put the Democrat lead on the generic ballot at 47% to 44%, half of what it was in mid-September. Republican leaders certainly have noticed. "I think we can keep the majority," Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) told Politico this week. "I think all of these races are margin of error, at least the ones that we have to win. And historically, at least if you look at polls, we tend to outperform them."

House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) made a similar case to Family Research Council President Tony Perkins on This Week on Capitol Hill after Cook Political Report shifted more seats toward Democrats.

"You know, the polling really is interesting when you dig into it," Scalise said. "You're seeing an undersampling of Republicans, and we're digging into some of these."

He added that Democrats promote rosy polls "because they want to depress conservative voters."

Of course, the warning signs for the GOP are real, and Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) admitted Tuesday that "this is going to be a very close election." But National Review's Jim Geraghty, who rarely plays the optimist about Republican prospects, explained why Americans should be wary of blue-wave talk, writing that "certain left-of-center media voices always tell them there will be a blue wave every November."

Does this mean Republicans will hold the House and Senate? No, not necessarily. But I think it does tell us that even the media aren't buying the narrative of the inevitable Democrat wave anymore.

news.title: Kelly, Gallego headed for presidential campaign collision | Exclusive
news.text:
Mark Kelly and Ruben Gallego are on a presidential campaign collision course. 

Both of Arizona’s Democratic senators are weighing presidential bids in 2028, hoping their ability to win in a right-leaning border state will open up a path to the White House. The dynamic already is setting them up to compete for endorsements, donors and, most importantly, votes. 

“We've had some very awkward conversations on five-hour flights about this. No, no, just kidding,” Gallego told The Arizona Republic in an exclusive interview. “No, no. We haven't, actually."

The Senate colleagues have not spoken about their presidential ambitions, Gallego said Oct. 8.

He doesn’t expect they will anytime soon. 

“We're probably gonna just like, dance around it forever. Until, you know, one of us blinks first. And then we'll have a conversation,” Gallego said. “Come on, politicians are passive-aggressive. You know how that's gonna end up.”

Kelly and Gallego have been here before. Gallego was gearing up for a 2020 Senate bid until Kelly got in the race. Gallego passed to avoid a “spirited and nasty primary,” he told The Republic in 2019.

This cycle, though, Gallego doesn’t seem as deterred by the potentially combustible dynamic — or the nearly $25 million Kelly reported in his campaign bank account at the end of June. 

Both lawmakers are laying the groundwork to join what’s likely to be a jam-packed presidential primary field.

They’re hardly alone. 

Big-name Democrats such as former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, and Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker are among the possible candidates. 

There could be multiple Californians in the race, too. Democrats Rep. Ro Khanna, former Vice President Kamala Harris and Gov. Gavin Newsom hail from the same state and are considered could-be candidates, though Newsom drew a line and said he won’t run if Harris does. 

Still, it’s unusual for two senators from the same state to seek the presidential nomination. In fact, it hasn’t been done in nearly six decades, according to presidential historian Douglas Brinkley.

Two Minnesotans — Vice President and former Sen. Hubert Humphrey and sitting Sen. Eugene McCarthy — ran for the Democratic nomination in 1968. The race didn’t exactly end on great terms: McCarthy refused to endorse Humphrey at the Democratic National Convention and only begrudgingly voted for him over Republican Richard Nixon in November.

So far, Kelly and Gallego have given each other a wide berth. In fact, Kelly declined to comment for this story. 

But they can’t avoid each other forever, or even for very much longer. 

“It's in everybody's interest to get along,” said state Rep. Sean Bagniewski, an Iowa lawmaker who Kelly and Gallego are both courting. Iowa is no longer Democrats' first-in-the-nation caucus state, but it's still a popular stop for White House aspirants.

Bagniewski said he has known Gallego for almost a decade, since he came to Iowa to stump for Democrats in 2018. More recently, Bagniewski showed Kelly around downtown Des Moines in August. 

Kelly returned the favor and invited Bagniewski to Tucson for a young leaders meetup. The former Polk County Democrats chair will fly into Arizona this week to attend.

The Arizona White House rivals are even bumping into each other on policy ideas.

Gallego spoke to The Republic a day after he released a new, sweeping economic proposal. The first-term senator proposed raising the minimum wage to $20, making companies pay double for overtime and putting new restrictions on data centers and artificial intelligence firms.

Gallego’s 32-plan middle class jobs plan was reminiscent of a presidential campaign platform, full of pictures and biographical information about Arizona’s junior senator. 

He released the plan two weeks after Kelly unveiled his own pitch to protect workers from AI upheaval. Both lawmakers floated expanding unemployment to 26 weeks and making states cover 75% of missed wages. 

Gallego said he’s still deciding whether to seek the White House in 2028, noting that he has a young family to consider. As for Kelly, Gallego said there’s room for both Arizona senators in the presidential primary field. 

“There's always room for more people to do anything,” Gallego said. “If I do anything, it's because I think it's the best first, for my family, and two, the best thing I can do for my country.” 

Kelly has amped up travel to presidentially relevant states and spoken openly about considering a campaign, while Gallego’s presidential ambitions stalled for several months. 

Gallego’s penchant for spending campaign cash on childcare and luxury trips to donor retreats with his family in tow landed his leadership PAC a Justice Department subpoena, Politico reported. Gallego’s office has brushed off the DOJ probe as politically motivated.

Plus, Gallego has been burdened by his close friendship with disgraced former Rep. Eric Swalwell, D-California. Gallego initially defended Swalwell when rumors were swirling about his ex-best friend, then he denounced Swalwell after multiple women accused the California Democrat of sexual misconduct. 

The typically tight-lipped Kelly used his colleague's missteps as an opportunity to draw a contrast in July. The resulting back-and-forth was an early glimpse into what Kelly and Gallego could sound like as adversaries in 2028. 

Kelly knocked Gallego’s judgment for endorsing Swalwell and Graham Platner, the Maine Democrat with a Nazi-like tattoo who was forced out of a pivotal Senate race after a woman accused him of rape. 

“I didn't endorse either of them,” Kelly said. “This job requires judgment.”

Gallego adviser Chuck Rocha hit right back when he caught wind of what Kelly had said. In Rocha’s view, Americans are hungry for someone who speaks their mind, even if that means “being too quick here or there.” 

“What Mark Kelly's talking about is the status quo," Rocha said. “And I can promise you people are getting fed up with that (expletive).” 

Stephanie Murray covers national politics and the Trump administration for The Arizona Republic and azcentral.com. She co-hosts “The Gaggle,” The Republic’s weekly politics podcast. Reach her at stephanie.murray@usatodayco.com, on X and TikTok @stephanie_murr and on Instagram @stephaniemurray.news.

news.text: Less than a month before the midterm elections, President Donald Trump's net approval rating is underwater in most states. Trump has a negative net approval rating in 39 states, according to the latest figures. Republicans are concerned about losing control of Congress, and polls show Democrats gaining ground. The data comes from Civiqs' rolling online tracker, based on 135,005 responses from registered voters collected between January 20, 2025, and October 8, 2026. Key Points Why It Matters Republicans are seeking to retain control of Congress in November's midterm elections, with Democrats hoping to make gains in the Senate and House. If Democrats win both chambers, they could significantly restrict the president's ability to pass legislation during the final two years of his presidency. Trump's negative net approval ratings across much of the country offer a snapshot of the political climate heading into the elections, although presidential approval does not predict how voters will cast their ballots in individual races. Polls also consistently underestimated Trump's support ahead of the past three presidential elections, meaning his true levels of support could be higher than the latest polls reflect. Trump’s Positive Approval Rating in 11 States Trump's net approval rating is positive in 11 states, all of which are typically Republican-leaning. His highest net approval rating is in Wyoming (+14), North Dakota (+11), West Virginia (+10) and Arkansas (+8). The remaining states in which he has a net positive rating are by narrow margins, between +1 and +4. Trump Underwater Ahead of Key Senate Races Trump has a negative net approval rating in six states where Republicans hold Senate seats that Democrats seek to flip. Trump's net approval rating is negative in Maine (-32), Texas (-20), Iowa (-21), Ohio (-18) and Alaska (-16). The Cook Political Report classifies these races as toss-ups. While Trump lost Maine to then-Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election, he won the other four states by double-digit margins. Democrats are also targeting North Carolina's Republican-held Senate seat, which the Cook Political Report rates as a likely Democratic win. Trump's net approval rating in the state is -18. Michigan is the only state with a Democratic-held seat that Cook considers a toss-up. Trump's net approval rating in the Wolverine State is -26. In Kansas, the only state with a toss-up Senate race to give the president a positive job rating, Trump's net approval rating is +1. Red States Turn Negative on Trump Trump's net approval is lower in every state than it was on January 20, 2025, when he took office for his second term. His approval rating has recently turned negative in several states where it was steadily positive until earlier this year. Tennessee (-4), Nebraska (-4) and Indiana (-6) had positive net approval ratings until July or August, while Louisiana (-10) and Kentucky (-12) were positive until March. South Carolina (-9) hovered around zero in the first few months of the year before turning consistently negative in late March. In Mississippi (-6), Trump's rating fluctuated around zero in the spring before remaining negative from June onward. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: John Fitzpatrick and Shakeema Edwards.
news.summary: Trump's approval rating has turned negative in several Republican-leaning states ahead of November's midterm elections.

news.title: Factbox-US House races to watch in the 2026 elections
news.text:
By Nolan D. McCaskill

WASHINGTON, Oct 12 (Reuters) - Republicans in the US House of Representatives are defending a narrow majority in November's midterm elections. History suggests Democrats will gain seats - they would need to net four to win control of the chamber. But Republicans kickstarted a national redistricting battle that could make Democrats' path to a majority slightly more difficult.

Here are some races to watch: 

CAN LAWLER DEFY TRUMP'S GRAVITY?

US Representative Mike Lawler of New York is one of just three Republicans who represent a congressional district Kamala Harris won in 2024. The others are an open seat in Nebraska and a Pennsylvania district US Representative Brian Fitzpatrick is favored to win. That makes Lawler the most vulnerable House Republican up for reelection.

His opponent, Cait Conley, is a combat veteran and national security expert. Democrats have outspent Republicans by about $1 million in this district, but Lawler has a nearly five-to-one cash advantage over Conley.

Two polls conducted in late September show both Lawler and Conley with narrow leads in this toss-up race.

REPUBLICAN REDISTRICTING MAY GO SOUTH IN TEXAS

When Texas Republicans kicked off a national gerrymandering war against Democrats in the hopes of defying historical trends to hold their fragile majority in Washington, they sought to pick up five seats. Yet as Election Day nears, three of those seats are in play - all in South Texas. 

Democratic US Representatives Vicente Gonzalez and Henry Cuellar are now running in districts President Donald Trump would have won by 10 percentage points in 2024. The third district, which was redrawn from a safe Democratic seat into one Trump also would have carried by 10 points, is an open race between Republican Carlos De La Cruz and Democrat Johnny Garcia.

Gonzalez faces Republican Eric Flores, a former Texas Army National Guard infantry captain and former assistant US attorney. Gonzalez has nearly $2 million more in cash than Flores, and Democrats have spent twice as much to hold the seat as Republicans have spent to flip it. 

DAVIS TRIES TO DEFY A NORTH CAROLINA GERRYMANDER 

Republicans redrew Democratic US Representative Don Davis' district, shifting it from a North Carolina district Trump won by 3 points to one he would have carried by double digits.

Davis is seeking reelection anyway. He has outraised his opponent, retired Army Colonel Laurie Buckhout, and reported more cash on hand. Buckhout has largely self-funded her campaign. 

A poll released this week showed Davis with a 10-point lead over Buckhout. Democrats have significantly outspent Republicans in this district, $5.8 million to just $600,000. 

A GOLDEN FLIP IN MAINE?

The retirement of centrist Democratic US Representative Jared Golden in a district Trump won by 9 points in 2024 opened a key flip opportunity for Republicans. Former Maine Governor Paul LePage is running against progressive state Auditor Matt Dunlap. 

LePage led in fundraising through June, more than doubling Dunlap's $1.2 million and reporting nearly $1.5 million more cash. House Democrats' campaign arm added Dunlap to its "Red to Blue" program for top offensive opportunities in August. 

Polls this month showed Dunlap with a slim lead over LePage.

HIGH HOPES IN OHIO

US Representative Max Miller of Ohio was reelected by 15 points in 2024, though an independent candidate got 13% of the vote. Trump won the district by a smaller margin than Miller, and domestic and child abuse allegations have made the congressman uniquely vulnerable.

Miller has denied the allegations, but US Senator Bernie Moreno, a fellow Ohio Republican, has called on him to resign and end his reelection campaign. Moreno's daughter is Miller's ex-wife. 

The once safe seat is now seen as a toss-up. Brian Poindexter, the Democratic nominee, is an ironworker, a Brook Park city councilor and a member of Democrats' Red to Blue program. Democrats have poured $3.4 million into flipping the seat, compared to Republicans' $730,000.

THIRD TIME'S A CHARM IN IOWA?

US Representative Mariannette Miller-Meeks of Iowa faces a familiar opponent in former state Representative Christina Bohannan, a Democrat who ran unsuccessfully against Miller-Meeks in 2022 and 2024. This time, however, could be different.

Trump is deeply unpopular, and the combination of tariffs and the war in Iran has elevated cost-of-living concerns. Trump's policies have driven up the price of diesel and fertilizer as voters have said affordability is their top issue this cycle.

Miller-Meeks and Bohannan posted nearly identical fundraising hauls of $7 million through June 30, but Bohannan entered July with a cash advantage of more than $730,000. Fundraising reports due next week will show where each campaign stands financially through September. But Democrats have outspent Republicans here by more than $3 million.

SOUTH FLORIDA REPUBLICAN BREAKS WITH TRUMP ON IMMIGRATION

"Mr. President, some of your immigration efforts have gone too far." That warning came last month from an incumbent Republican, US Representative Maria Elvira Salazar of Florida, who represents a district Trump won by nearly 15 points in 2024.

Salazar is still favored to win reelection, but her high-profile break with the president on a signature issue is a sign Republicans could lose ground with the Latino voters who helped return Trump to the White House. 

Like Salazar, her opponent, Eliott Rodriguez, is a former TV news anchor. Democrats added Rodriguez to their Red to Blue program last week but haven't invested much money in his race, though they've outspent Republicans by about $280,000.

A poll conducted last month showed Salazar with a narrow lead within the margin of error.

WILL VOTERS SEND MGP BACK TO WASHINGTON?

US Representative Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington authored a resolution condemning a fellow Democrat and helped Republicans advance their agenda by bucking her party on traditionally party-line procedural votes. That may help her in a district Trump narrowly won in 2024.

Gluesenkamp Perez finished second in Washington's top-two primary, trailing state Senate Republican Leader John Braun. Gluesenkamp Perez has a $4 million fundraising advantage over Braun, but Republicans have outspent Democrats by more than $1 million. 

A poll conducted in September showed Braun leading by 1 percentage point. The two debated for the first time on Wednesday.

DEMOCRATS RAISING THE BAR IN KENTUCKY?

Democrats only hold one of Kentucky's six US House seats. But they see an opening in the 6th District, where incumbent Representative Andy Barr is the Republican nominee for US Senate.

The Republican nominee is Ralph Alvarado, a former Kentucky state senator and ex-head of the Tennessee health department. His opponent is Democrat Zach Dembo, an ex-Navy JAG officer and former federal prosecutor.

There's little daylight between the candidates in fundraising, and both parties have poured roughly the same amount of money into the race.

The latest polls, all of which were sponsored by Democrats, show Dembo leading. Trump won the district by 15 points in 2024.

MAY THE BEST DEM WIN

California's top-two primary system occasionally pits two members of the same party against each other in a general election. This year, US Representatives Ken Calvert and Young Kim — both Republicans — are running for the same seat after Democrats redrew the state's congressional map. 

US Representative Doris Matsui, a Democrat, is similarly facing Sacramento City Councilor Mai Vang, a democratic socialist. Matsui is backed by the Democratic establishment, including the state party, Governor Gavin Newsom, both US senators and 37 members of California's congressional delegation.

The outcome won't affect the balance of power in the House, but it could affect the makeup of a future Democratic majority. Several progressive or democratic socialist candidates have ousted mainstream or moderate Democrats in primaries this year, giving the left wing of the party significant momentum heading into a presidential election cycle in 2028. 

 (Reporting by Nolan D. McCaskill; Editing by Michael Learmonth and Daniel Wallis)

news.title: Republican Steve Hilton leans on cheeky ads, voter discontent in long-shot campaign for governor
news.text: In rural Modoc County, in California's remote northeast corner, Republican gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton donned a beige cowboy hat and climbed atop a horse. Riding through a grassy field, with his dress shoes in the stirrups, Hilton lamented to a camera that California was "completely being ruined by killjoy bureaucrats" who put too many rules on fun stuff like beach fire pits and bars that stay open extra late. In coastal San Luis Obispo County, Hilton boarded a bright yellow dune buggy at the Oceano Dunes State Vehicular Recreation Area and called the California Coastal Commission "idiots" for trying to end off-road beach driving. And in the Central Valley, he waved the ceremonial green flag at a stock car race at the Madera Speedway, where he was named grand marshal of the annual Harvest Classic. (The designation caused a minor uproar, prompting the operator of the racetrack to make a fake online concession menu that offered a hot dog and soda for $6 for Republicans and $17.50 for Democrats.) If it seems like Hilton — the British immigrant and former Fox News talk show host — is just about everywhere, taking just about every media interview that comes his way, well, that's the point, he says. He has logged thousands of miles on the proverbial campaign trail, visiting all 58 counties in his quest to lead the nation's most populous state, where no Republican has been elected to statewide office in 20 years. Meanwhile, his heavily favored — and far more staid — opponent, Democrat Xavier Becerra, has kept a comparatively low profile, agreeing to just one debate with Hilton and holding few public events, mostly in urban areas. In a phone interview while driving through Los Angeles, Hilton said: "Whether I'm in Humboldt or Del Norte or Siskiyou County, my joke is, when people say, 'Where do you live?' I say I live in the Hampton Inn somewhere in California because we're basically in a different place every night." The odds are against him. Sure, California produced GOP presidents Richard Nixon and Ronald Reagan. But today, Democrats outnumber Republicans nearly 2 to 1 in the state, and the current White House occupant shares a mutual disdain with the vast majority of Golden State voters. Hilton was endorsed during the primary by President Trump, who suggested at a campaign rally this month that Iran could "take out" Los Angeles and San Diego, drawing swift outrage from both Democrats and Republicans. Hilton has tried to walk a fine line, appealing to the 6 million Californians who voted for the president in 2024 while simultaneously downplaying Trump's support. This summer, Hilton took out full-page ads in The Times and the San Francisco Chronicle asking: "Can you be anti-Trump and still vote for me?" "Yes, I'm the Republican," it said. "The 'Fox News guy.' Endorsed by Trump. But this election is not about who you hate in Washington. It's about what you love here." Corrin Rankin, chairwoman of the California Republican Party, said that 16 years after the state's last Republican governor, Arnold Schwarzenegger, left office, "it's safe to say Democrats own all the problems in California." "You can't blame Trump for what's going on here in California," she said. "We feel really good about Steve Hilton's campaign. He is working so hard, up and down the state." Hilton has blasted California Democrats as entitled, saying they assume Becerra will cruise to victory in the race to replace termed-out Gov. Gavin Newsom simply because he has a "D" beside his name on the Nov. 3 ballot. Hilton frequently quotes a September podcast interview by Los Angeles' Democratic mayor, Karen Bass, who mocked his British accent and said: "The governor's race right now is over. Our governor's name is Xavier Becerra. You don't need an election on Nov. 3. A Republican cannot win in this state." Hilton told The Times that Democrats "feel they don't have to earn your vote. ... They can deliver results that are bad as ever, and they don't need to work hard to deliver results for people or earn their support. And I think it's that attitude that is going to be their downfall." Becerra is a former member of Congress who represented Los Angeles, and he was the California attorney general and U.S. Health and Human Services secretary under President Biden. He has the backing of 58% of likely California voters, compared with 33% who support Hilton, according to a poll released late last month by the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies and co-sponsored by The Times. The poll showed that voters' top concern was reducing the state's high cost of living — followed by fighting Trump administration policies. Jonathan Underland, a spokesman for the Becerra campaign, said, "Trump has browbeaten his way into the California political discourse" with his mass deportation raids, his willingness to stonewall federal wildfire relief funds for political reasons, and his aggressive tariffs that many blame for driving up costs nationwide. “Hilton is trying to win an election, so he tries to frame himself as someone who can appeal to the broader electorate," Underland said. "But at the end of the day, he has the albatross around his neck, which is Trump, who is openly hostile to California." Hilton cuts a colorful and pugnacious figure on the campaign trail. He eschews ties and jackets, favoring T-shirts with punchy phrases like, "$ave With Steve" and "WAKE UP" superimposed on a California license plate — a reference to his proposal to eliminate the state's Department of Motor Vehicles and slash vehicle registration fees, which would cut billions in state revenue. He wears one bracelet with the name of slain right-wing activist Charlie Kirk, whom he called an "incredibly close friend." Another reads, "Save Girls' Sports," calling back to this spring, when he traveled to the state high school track and field championship in Clovis to protest the participation of a transgender athlete. Hilton, 57, was born in London to parents who fled conflict in their native Hungary during the 1956 uprising against the Soviet-controlled communist government and later anglicized their surname, Hircsák, to Hilton. He was a senior advisor to British Prime Minister David Cameron, a member of the Conservative Party, though the men's once-close friendship never recovered from Brexit, Britain’s withdrawal from the European Union. Hilton supported it; Cameron did not. Hilton earned a reputation as eccentric but savvy, pushing the Conservative Party to embrace same-sex marriage and more climate-friendly policies. Dubbed "the barefoot revolutionary" for his refusal to wear shoes, Hilton was satirized on the BBC political sitcom "The Thick of It" as Stewart Pearson, the Tories' “eco-friendly, media-savvy, blue-sky-thinking” communications director. He and his family moved to California in 2012 after his wife, Rachel Whetstone, was promoted to lead global communications at Google. For six years, he hosted "The Next Revolution," a weekly Fox News show from which Trump regularly tweeted clips. In 2015, the couple purchased their home in the Silicon Valley city of Atherton, one of the wealthiest ZIP Codes in the U.S., for $12.5 million, property records show. Whetstone now leads communications for Sierra, an AI startup founded by OpenAI board Chairman Bret Taylor and Clay Bavor, who met while working at Google. Hilton and Whetstone's 2024 tax returns show they had a combined household income of $7.5 million, which included his reported earnings of $250,000 from Fox News and her $6.7 million from her then-employer, Netflix. Hilton became a U.S. citizen in 2021 and last year renounced his British citizenship. He finished second in the June 2 primary behind Becerra. Under California's top-two primary system, the first- and second-place finishers, regardless of party, advance to the general election. The pack of Democratic candidates was so large that party leaders initially urged struggling candidates — including Becerra — to drop out to avoid splitting the vote. Becerra shot to the top of the polls when then-Rep. Eric Swalwell, a front-runner at the time, dropped out of the race after he was accused of sexual assault and misconduct. Republicans coalesced around Hilton after the president endorsed him over his GOP rival, Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco, a staunch Trump supporter who later said the endorsement made Hilton unelectable. Kim Nalder, director of the Project for an Informed Electorate at Sacramento State, said it is exceedingly difficult for Hilton to distance himself from Trump and the Fox News brand. "If you had a different brand of Republican they might have a shot," given the discontent in the state over myriad issues, she said. "But Trump is so politically radioactive in California right now that it is an effective technique to tie this particular candidate to him." The governor's race comes as Californians are deeply frustrated by the state's exorbitant housing costs, top-in-the-nation gasoline prices and high taxes, as well as its entrenched homelessness crisis. California's population growth is stagnant after years of pandemic-era losses, with immigration lagging amid the Trump administration's crackdown and many residents leaving the state for more affordable parts of the country. Greg Perrone, past president of the conservative Greater Bakersfield Republican Assembly, said he was impressed with Hilton's policy knowledge and the amount of detail in his economic plans. “There’s a real concern that the current state of the economy is worse than people expected," Perrone said. "A lot of people hung their hat on Donald Trump saying he was going to bring down prices, and that just has not happened. There's a lot of angst." Perrone said he remains a Trump supporter, though he has been frustrated by the frenetic roll-out of tariffs that, he said, hurt many businesses. While he has been annoyed that Becerra, in his view, has focused more on the president than laying out his own detailed economic plans, he acknowledged that the strategy plays well in blue California. Christopher Cole, former chairman of the Lassen County Republican Party, said that in his rural corner of the state, he has seen Trump banners that have hung since 2016 start to come down because people are angry about the Iran war, the high cost of fuel and the economy. "When Trump stupidly endorsed Hilton, it was the kiss of death for any down-ticket Republican,” said Cole, whose county voted for Trump on 76% of the ballots in 2024, the highest percentage in the state, and was the only one to support Bianco in this year's primary. "Hilton is a carnival barker and a very wealthy man," said Cole, who supported Bianco. "You can’t run a multimillionaire when people are struggling to put food on the table.” Hilton has made a slew of campaign promises to lower the cost of living, including having no taxes on income below $150,000, lowering energy bills by slashing climate-friendly regulations imposed by Democrats, and having $3 gasoline (though governors cannot directly set the price at the pump, which is driven largely by global crude oil supply and demand). He has tried to channel the state's discontent into persuading voters to "try something different" by voting Republican. During the gubernatorial race debate on CNN last month, Hilton quoted a former Biden domestic policy advisor who reportedly called Becerra a "bitch-ass," and his campaign promptly launched a website, bitchassbecerra.com, outlining alleged failures of the politician known for his calm demeanor and decades of government experience. "I think Hilton got dealt a bad card with Becerra making the runoff," said Rob Stutzman, a Republican strategist who was Schwarzenegger's spokesman. "It's difficult to get anyone outraged about Becerra because he is perfectly boring. He worked for Joe Biden — maybe that upsets some people? — but you can't associate him with any bizarre, woke policies like you could Kamala Harris or Gavin Newsom." Hilton's campaign this month released a provocative, sexually suggestive ad titled "Just Try It!" in which two young women sit on a bed in a candlelit room. An LGBTQ+ pride flag hangs on the wall, and they're seemingly talking through one's first romantic encounter with another female. Wearing a T-shirt that says, "RESIST," the anti-MAGA mantra, the first-timer nervously says: "I've just never done anything like this before. Like, what if my dad finds out?" The other woman holds her hand as she fills out a ballot for Hilton then says, "Now lick it," referring to the mail ballot envelope. Some conservatives condemned the ad, saying it promoted lesbianism. Liberals criticized it, too, saying it was insensitive to the LGBTQ+ community. The day the ad launched, he told The Times: "I think there's a very strong sense that things aren't working in California, and my argument is: 'OK, let's try something different.'" Later, he said he never meant to offend anyone with the risqué ad, which did, after all, do its job in racking up millions of views online — coveted and invaluable publicity for a long-shot California Republican.
news.summary: Hilton has tried to walk a fine line, appealing to the 6 million Californians who voted for Donald Trump in 2024 while avoiding the president's brand.
news.author: Hailey Branson-Potts

news.title: Susan Collins Is in Stronger Shape Than Before Her Surprise 2020 Victory
news.text: Maine Republican Senator Susan Collins is entering the final weeks of her reelection campaign in a stronger position than she held before her surprise victory six years ago, even as powerful national headwinds threaten the Republican Party’s Senate majority. Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority, meaning Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take control of the chamber, because Vice President JD Vance would serve as tiebreaker in an evenly divided Senate. Maine and North Carolina are among their clearest opportunities, but winning both would not be enough: Democrats would also need to hold every seat they currently control and prevail in at least two more Republican-held states, with Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas among the expanded battlegrounds. Recent election models have made Democrats narrow favorites for Senate control, although the outcome remains highly uncertain and rests on several closely divided races. The broader political climate is unfavorable to Republicans. An Associated Press-NORC survey conducted from September 24 to 28 among 2,140 adults, with a plus or minus 2.9 percentage point margin of error, found that 31 percent of U.S. adults approved of President Donald Trump’s job performance, while only 26 percent approved of his handling of the economy and 17 percent approved of his approach to the cost of living. Civiqs’ national tracker also placed Trump at 34 percent approval and 60 percent disapproval among registered voters nationally on October 6. His net approval rating, calculated by subtracting disapproval from approval, stood at minus 34 among Maine registered voters in the Civiqs polling. Collins, however, has repeatedly demonstrated an ability to separate herself from the national Republican ticket in a state that Trump has never carried. And she is more competitive than she was at the same stage in 2020. Virtually every public poll late in the 2020 campaign showed Democratic challenger Sara Gideon ahead. The final polling average put Gideon at 46.4 percent and Collins at 42.6 percent, with major surveys regularly showing Collins four to six points behind. Collins nevertheless won by 8.6 points, taking 51 percent of the vote. This year’s polls still show a close race, but the latest surveys have moved modestly toward Jackson. The RealClearPolitics average on October 9 placed Democrat Troy Jackson at 48.3 percent and Collins at 47.3 percent. Its underlying polls ranged from a four-point Jackson lead to a three-point Collins advantage, with three recording ties. A Washington Post-Schar School poll released Friday placed Jackson ahead by 50 percent to 46 percent among 800 likely voters surveyed from September 30 to October 5. The margin of error was plus or minus 3.6 percentage points, placing Jackson’s advantage within the range of sampling error. That does not make Collins the favorite. It means she enters the decisive phase from a position she would have welcomed in 2020. The central question is whether Collins can again attract enough crossover support to separate her political identity from the Republican Party’s national standing. Newsweek emailed the Collins and Jackson campaigns for comment on Wednesday morning. Why Collins Looks Stronger Than in 2020 Three indicators distinguish Collins’ position from six years ago. First is polling. In 2020, she spent much of the campaign behind. This year, neither candidate has established a durable lead, and the RealClearPolitics average separates them by less than one point. Second is Collins’ personal standing. A September New York Times/Portland Press Herald/Siena Research Institute poll found that 51 percent viewed her favorably and 48 percent unfavorably. The poll surveyed 619 registered Maine voters from September 15 to 22, 2026, and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4.9 percentage points. A comparable poll six years earlier put her at 50 percent favorable and 47 percent unfavorable. That poll, which surveyed 663 likely voters, with a plus or minus 5.1-point margin of error, was conducted September 11 to 16, 2020. Her ratings were almost unchanged despite another Trump presidency, the overturning of Roe v. Wade, and years of partisan conflict. That stability matters because Collins relies on voters who do not consistently support Republicans. She does not need Trump to carry Maine. She needs enough independents and Democrats to see her as distinct from him and valuable to the state. Collins used Tuesday night’s first debate to reinforce the same argument, emphasizing both her independence from Trump and the practical benefits of her Senate seniority. She said she was "not exactly his favorite senator" and highlighted $1.5 billion in federal funding she said she had secured for 672 Maine projects over the past five years. Jackson sought to puncture that image, repeatedly linking her to Trump and challenging her over her vote to confirm Justice Brett Kavanaugh, asking voters: "Would you trust her to pick the next Supreme Court justice?" Their October 8 rematch focused heavily on Iran, energy prices and each candidate’s independence. Collins demanded an apology after Jackson accused her of benefiting financially from the war, an allegation for which he did not provide specific evidence during the debate. Collins also defended her record of opposing the conflict. Collins said she disagreed with Kavanaugh’s vote to overturn Roe v. Wade but continued to defend his confirmation. Third is money. Collins raised $26.5 million in 2020, compared with Gideon’s $68.6 million. Her principal campaign committee reported $16.2 million in receipts and $11 million in cash on hand for the 2025-26 cycle through June 30, according to Federal Election Commission (FEC) filings reviewed by Newsweek. The FEC cautions that newly filed data may take up to 48 hours to appear. Even so, Collins’ financial position gives her a structural advantage over an opponent who entered the race in July. A separate personal financial disclosure showed Jackson and his spouse holding assets worth between $147,000 and $430,000, compared with roughly $4 million to $10 million disclosed by Susan Collins and her spouse. Because congressional disclosures report assets in ranges, those figures should not be treated as precise net-worth estimates. Jackson’s campaign told Newsweek that the filing reflected "a lifetime of working for a paycheck," while Collins spokesperson Blake Kernen criticized his union consulting income and delayed filing. From an Oyster Farmer to a Fifth-Generation Logger The Democratic campaign began with Graham Platner, an oyster farmer, military veteran, and small-business owner from coastal Maine. Platner was raised in Sullivan and returned home in 2018 after serving in the Marine Corps and Maryland Army National Guard, including deployments to Iraq and Afghanistan. The following year, he took over Waukeag Neck Oyster Company, while also running a mooring service and serving as the town’s harbor master. His livelihood, shaped by cold water, weather and the health of the local ecosystem, gave physical form to his economic-populist message. By late May, Platner had become the overwhelming Democratic favorite. The University of New Hampshire Survey Center’s Pine Tree State Poll found that 76 percent of likely Democratic primary voters supported him, while 73 percent viewed him favorably. Those findings came from 595 likely primary voters and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. Among 1,280 likely general-election voters, Platner led Collins 51 percent to 42 percent, with a 2.7-point margin of error. The wider survey of 1,397 Maine residents was conducted online from May 21 to 25, 2026. Platner withdrew in July after allegations of sexual misconduct toward women, which he denied. A July 25 convention replaced him with Jackson, a fifth-generation logger from Allagash and former Maine Senate president. Jackson’s campaign says he worked 80-hour weeks in the woods and entered politics after joining loggers in a 1998 blockade at the Canadian border. Jackson could inherit Platner’s argument that corporations and wealthy interests were squeezing rural workers. What he could not inherit was time: he had little more than three months to build a statewide campaign against an incumbent who has held the seat since 1997. The Unresolved National Risk Maine rejected Trump in all three of his presidential campaigns. Kamala Harris carried the state by 6.9 points in 2024, while the Senate race is rated a toss-up. Jackson’s route is to make the contest a referendum on Trump, retain the Democratic coalition assembled by Platner and use his record as a logger and labor advocate to compete for rural and working-class voters. Collins must persuade Mainers that her seniority, influence and ability to secure federal funding outweigh dissatisfaction with the president and Republican Party when they head to the polls on November 3. Democrats produced one of the cycle’s most distinctive candidates, lost him after the primary and replaced him with another working-class populist. They have still not pushed Collins into the consistently weak polling position she occupied before her last victory. Collins enters the closing stretch with stronger polling and a much greater financial advantage than she had in 2020. The question is whether those advantages can withstand the national forces moving against her. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: John Fitzpatrick and James Debens
news.summary: Susan Collins trailed consistently before winning Maine in 2020. New polling shows why her 2026 contest may be different.
news.author: Sam Stevenson

news.title: Blue-state governor’s race defies expectations as Republican closes in: Power Rankings
news.text: Republicans are gaining ground in blue-leaning Oregon, where Fox News Power Rankings have shifted the governor's race toward the GOP as Democratic Gov. Tina Kotek faces a competitive rematch with Republican Christine Drazan. The shift from Likely Democrat to Lean Democrat reflects a competitive political environment in Oregon, where concerns over homelessness, housing, taxes, schools and the cost of living have created an opening for Republicans to end a more than four-decade losing streak in gubernatorial elections. Republicans are gaining ground in Oregon even as they face a rough national political environment marked by high gas and diesel prices, what polls show is an unpopular war in Iran and President Donald Trump's low approval ratings "This is something historic we're trying to pull off," Drazan said in a Fox News Digital interview. "It's been a long time and we're due we win." CHECK OUT THE LATEST FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS IN THE MIDTERM ELECTIONS Then-Vice President Kamala Harris carried Oregon by 14 points in the 2024 presidential election, and Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden won his 2022 re-election by 15 points. But gubernatorial showdowns in the northwestern state have traditionally been much closer contests. Drazan, a former GOP leader in the Oregon House, lost to Kotek by less than four points in 2022. After her defeat, she won a state House election in 2024 and returned to the legislature, serving again as minority leader before being appointed last year to the state Senate. "It's good to stay in the fight. I think Oregonians... recognized that I didn't leave, I didn't move to a different state, I didn't go hide. I got engaged again, went back into the legislature to serve my community," Drazan emphasized. "I think that that matters to people, that I am committed long-term to our state." The latest public opinion polls indicate a margin of error race in the Kotek-Drazan rematch. "People are starting to get to know me a little bit more and my leadership, and they're taking a closer look at whether or not Oregon is uniquely bad right now. It's not a national issue, it's here at home," Drazan said. "We're struggling right now locally. So, that's making this race tight." While Drazan is trying to keep her focus on Oregon and local issues, the Kotek campaign is aiming to anchor the GOP challenger to Trump, who is very unpopular in the state. DEMOCRATS THINK A BLUE WAVE IS FORMER - HERE ARE THREE FACTORS THAT COULD STOP IT Kotek Communications Director Federico Araujo told Fox News Digital, "There are still many undecided voters ahead of November. But when the choice is clear in an election, they always show up. And the choice couldn't be any clearer in this race: Christine Drazan is ready to open the door to Trump's agenda and Governor Kotek is fighting every day to protect Oregonians from federal overreach and harm." But Drazan said that "Oregon needs change. Oregon needs to be done with one approach to the world. Single-party control has not been good for us in my home state. And we need that balance." "We need people to be at the table that have been ignored in the past to be able to turn our economy around, frankly, and turn our schools around and serve the people that are facing addiction and slowly dying on our streets. Those are significant challenges, and Tina Kotek doesn't have the answers to solve them," she charged. Four years ago, Drazan received plenty of support from national Republicans as her party benefited from a more favorable political environment. DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB This time around national Republicans are facing stiff headwinds as they work to hang on to their fragile congressional majorities and governors offices across the country. But the Drazan campaign says it's now landing financial support from the Republican Governors Association. "I am grateful to have the Republican Governors Association as a partner in this race. They are investing in this race now," Drazan said. But she noted "the sitting governor has a fundraising advantage that's significant today," and added "I could always use more support." Democratic Governors Association Spokesperson Johanna Warshaw spotlighted the competitive nature of Oregon gubernatorial showdowns, but told Fox News Digital, "Governor Kotek has the advantage and we're confident she'll win. "Clearly, the RGA agrees as they're leaving Christine Drazan's broke campaign out to dry," Warshaw claimed. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Drazan highlighted that she's "actively fundraising all the time and encouraging folks to get involved in this race right now. We have no limits in Oregon, and that allows me to be able to compete head to head." And pointing to her campaign, she said, "I want to achieve something extraordinary."
news.summary: Christine Drazan aims to end Oregon's four-decade GOP losing streak in a tight rematch with Democratic Gov. Tina Kotek over local issues.

news.title: GOP faces ire from workers who have lost jobs to tariffs
news.text:
NEW YORK -- Republicans are confronting a backlash over the tariffs that President Donald Trump made a cornerstone of his economic agenda, promising that charging higher taxes on imports would spur a factory renaissance in the United States. Although the country has added manufacturing jobs so far this year, the sector has fewer employees than when Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.

Nelson Vandermeer voted Republican for decades but balked at supporting Trump, fearing that the Republican's plan for tariffs on imports would hurt workers more than help.

Last year, Vandermeer's premonition came true in a very personal way. The 62-year-old lost his job as a product designer at Howard Miller, a clockmaker that relied on parts produced overseas. After a century in business, the company in Zeeland, Mich., closed its factory, sold off its inventory and brand name and laid off nearly 200 workers.

"So much for bringing jobs back," Vandermeer said. Next month, he plans to vote straight Democrat in the midterms.

White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers insisted that a factory boom is underway, citing increases in manufacturing output and more work in certain nonresidential construction trades. "Factory construction jobs of today mean more manufacturing jobs down the road once those factories come online," she said.

Even before the tariffs, Howard Miller struggled as Americans lost their taste for fancy timepieces such as its signature grandfather and mantel clocks. So the company broadened its offerings years ago to include bar carts, cabinets and consoles.

But those products also depended on glass and other parts from abroad, and diversification did not ensure survival.

"I could still have a job, but now I don't because of tariffs," Vandermeer said. "It was like taking a knife to the back."

Vandermeer lives in Michigan's 4th Congressional District, which is represented by Republican Bill Huizenga, who is running for a ninth term in the Nov. 3 election.

Before Trump implemented his broadest set of tariffs last year, on what the president called "Liberation Day," Huizenga was supportive.

"Is it going to be easy? Not necessarily. Is it the right thing to do? Absolutely it is," he told reporters at the time.

A spokesperson for Huizenga said last week that the congressman "sees a potential role for tariffs" for boosting domestic manufacturing "while recognizing the need to address their broader economic effects." His Democratic opponent, state Sen. Sean McCann, has criticized the incumbent for opposing legislation that would rein in tariffs that Trump imposed unilaterally.

There are similar issues in competitive races in Kansas, Iowa and Ohio, where Republican acquiescence could hurt the party on Election Day as their constituents face factory layoffs, farm foreclosures and higher prices.

Tracy Chew, 55, voted for Trump in 2016, then for Democrat Joe Biden in 2020 and Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024.

She used to work for Case, a backhoe manufacturer, but the company announced before the tariffs that it would close its plant in Burlington, Iowa. She lost her job in April, as did her daughter, followed by husband and son-in-law over the next few weeks.

Chew is leaning toward voting for Democrats again this year, feeling that Trump let them down.

"I'm furious he isn't doing enough," she said. "Tariffs are not targeting the right companies, the right amount."

Layoffs in Iowa have piled up elsewhere.

Winnebago Industries, which produces recreational vehicles like campers, cut 200 jobs last year after the cost of importing aluminum, steel and electronics increased by tens of millions of dollars.

"It's a day to day battle," said Michael Happe, the company's chief executive.

Tariffs are far from the only reason for the lost of manufacturing jobs, and factories have cut workers for decades with or without them. Even some Republicans who dislike Trump's approach will not split with the party.

Bicycle Corp. of America, which closed its factory in South Carolina last year, blamed rising prices for imported parts. Koby Bird, who retired after working in quality control, likes tariffs but was frustrated by Trump's habit of raising and lowering them seemingly at whim.

"It was all over the place," Bird said. "Businesses couldn't plan."

Next month, Bird is likely to stick with Republicans, including U.S. Sen. Darline Graham, because tariffs are only one issue and he believes Democrats would spend too much money on the wrong things.
news.author: Bernard Condon The Associated Press

news.title: OPINION | BRADLEY GITZ: Ruminations on this and that
news.text:
Because there are sometimes too many topics to cover in just one; we have columns like this one.

The remarkable story of FlyDubai Flight 1073 should remind us of the profound differences between Israel and its unsavory neighbors.

Israelis don't try to hijack airplanes in order to crash them and kill all the innocent men, women, and children on board. To the contrary, no country in our time has been more threatened by terrorism or fought back against it so heroically.

Even though our viscerally anti-Israel media seeks to convince us otherwise (usually by reflexively spewing Hamas propaganda), we should never be confused as to who the good guys and bad guys are here.

Our relationship with Israel isn't a geopolitical liability but a tremendous asset. Israel remains a valuable ally in a crucial strategic region, as well as an oasis of democracy, progress and civilization surrounded by despotism, stagnation, and barbarism.

As if Oct. 7 wasn't sufficient for clarity on the matter.

If antisemitism is rising on both the left and right, we should take care to note that on the latter it is largely confined to bizarre fringe podcasters (Tucker Carlson, Nick Fuentes, Candace Owens, etc.), whereas on the former, within the Democratic Party, it is becoming something of a foundational ideological element.

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro might be the Democrat with the best chance of winning the presidency in 2028 but has little chance of ever winning the nomination for the sole reason that he is Jewish (the same reason Donald Trump claims he was rejected by Kamala Harris as her running mate two years ago).

That almost all of the candidates from the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) winning Democratic primaries across the country are virulently anti-Israel makes it difficult to not sense antisemitism lurking behind their socialism; to the extent the DSA becomes more influential in Democratic Party politics, so too does antisemitism (and yes, being anti-Israel to the point of denying it has a right to exist is antisemitic).

In short, and while survey research shows Republicans still side overwhelmingly with Israel, Democrats now overwhelmingly side with Israel's enemies (which, objectively speaking, means the side of Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran).

According to a recent CNN poll, a remarkable 53 percent of self-identified Republicans say that Trump is the Republican president they admire most, compared to just 18 percent for Ronald Reagan and 8 percent for Abe Lincoln (with presumably hardly any support for Dwight Eisenhower or Teddy Roosevelt).

The "recency effect" always influences such polling results (even Joe Biden might have scored well among Democrats in response to such a query during his presidency) and it's likely many of the respondents weren't even alive when Reagan was president (and, given the abysmal level of historical knowledge, might never have heard of Eisenhower and confuse Teddy for Franklin).

Still, it might finally be time for a rethinking here, as with so much else related to Trump, beginning with the possibility that his behavior, with all its pettiness and narcissism and irrationality, might actually be appealing in many ways to contemporary Republicans rather than an embarrassment to be looked away from; that he is more an entertainer performing for them than a president interested in governing.

Maybe the problem isn't so much Trump, who might have simply identified and exploited a political market niche, as it is the nature of his supporters, such that the more outrageously he behaves the more popular he becomes with them.

National Review magazine, The Wall Street Journal and other bastions of traditional ("Reagan") conservatism can consistently denounce Trump in the harshest terms, but it doesn't mean anything any longer for his support within the GOP, if it ever did, as criticism from such quarters is simply taken as validation of his virtue.

The reasons the rest of us criticize Trump are the reasons MAGA Republicans love him.

Our politics have become so unserious and performative and dumbed down because (a) the voters as a whole have become dumber over time, increasingly viewing politics as a form of reality TV, and (b) the dumbest among those dumber voters have become the politically most influential.

A powerful inverse relationship exists between intelligence and seriousness in politics on one hand and political extremism on the other.

Unfortunately, the extremist fringes that now control our parties are where we are most likely to find the most uninformed and least serious people, which is another way of saying that the worst elements in American politics are now largely in charge of it.

And we wonder why so little of it makes sense.

It thus becomes incumbent upon the more serious and intelligent in each party, meaning the people interested in actually solving problems and who understand how democracy works within our constitutional order, to make common cause and push back against the dumbest, most extreme elements on their own side.

Finally, it is long past time for our president to take up drinking, perhaps heavily.

That way, when he posts all that bizarre stuff on social media in the wee hours of the morning, we can believe he's drunk rather than bat-crap crazy.

Freelance columnist Bradley R. Gitz, who lives in Batesville, received his Ph.D. in political science from the University of Illinois.

news.title: The blue wave looks real until you look a little closer
news.text: It’s like watching some sci-fi game with players competing on 470 different fields. Which is your basic definition of crazytown. No human being, without mainlining AI into his or her arm, could possibly track so many contests, so we bounce from one race to the next, with buzzers and bells, like a pinball machine. Look! Charlie Cook is moving 18 House races in the Democrats’ favor! This is o-vah! The blue wave is getting stronger. Put a cork in this one, it’s done! But wait a minute. The Republicans have a huge cash advantage. Big-time Democratic donors, for whatever reason, are sitting on their checkbooks. Don’t they realize the stakes? Are they all blinded by the sun on their private islands? There seems to be a consensus, even privately among Republicans, that the Dems will take the House. The only question is the margin. So we all wind-surf across the Senate race, even if we know little more than what we read that morning in Politico, or the New York Times or Wall Street Journal. The GOP just sent another $30 million to Ken Paxton, the Texas Republican who has more baggage than a 747. (Being impeached by your own party doesn’t help.) He was caught on audio saying "everybody’s numbers dropped" after President Trump’s midterm convention. Even Trump calls him "a pain in the *ss sometimes." And this is the guy they want to win? DEMOCRATS THINK A BLUE WAVE IS BUILDING. HERE ARE 3 FORCES THAT COULD STOP IT His Democratic opponent, James Talarico, went into hiding–what’s up with that? Turns out he had a nasty case of the flu. Still, it’s Texas, the Lone Star State, where Democratic dreams go to die. Okay, we’re starting to get vertigo. In Maine, is this the year Susan Collins gets knocked off? One poll has her trailing by four points against Democrat Troy Jackson, who replaced weirdo candidate and Nazi tattoo-wearing Graham Platner, who quit after a sexual assault allegation. What a lovely business. Republicans have a president who’s polling in the low 30s, which perhaps explains why he was campaigning the other day in Syracuse, when New York is among the bluest of blue states. The Democrats need a net gain of four seats to control the Senate, and while some are prematurely sipping Champagne, nobody really knows if they can draw that kind of inside straight. If they tell you they do, they’re lying. MICHIGAN SENATE DEBATE ERUPTS INTO PERSONAL ATTACKS AS ROGERS, EL-SAYED CLASH OVER ISRAEL, IRAN AND MORE There’s a harsh spotlight on the Michigan Senate race, featuring Democratic socialist Abdul el-Sayed vs. former congressman Mike Rogers. I eagerly watched their high-decibel debate the other night–okay, I was assigned to it--and here’s my takeaway. El-Sayed won on points–he’s just a smoother and more aggressive debater than Rogers, who looks like a classic pol–and every third sentence was an attack on Trump or the war. This put Rogers at a disadvantage, because he supported the Iran war but now says it should end. And El-Sayed kept whacking Rogers for owning two yachts, which is sort of irrelevant. Rogers called his opponent a "con man" and kept trying to tie him to the Muslim Brotherhood. This was a weakness for el-Sayed, who was asked whether he’d send aid if Israel was attacked, and insisted that he’d rather spend the money here at home. El-Sayed also did a lousy job of defending Medicare for All and why it wouldn’t bring the end of private insurance. Since Michigan is near the border, both men came out against Canadian tariffs–a flip for Rogers–in a noisy segment that was utterly indecipherable to mere mortals. The whole thing turned into an interrup-ta-thon, with the moderator constantly scolding the contenders. Aren’t you glad you missed it? Now, thanks to yours truly, you can pretend you saw the debate. But enough about the midterms. Time to join the punditocracy and speculate about 2028. Kamala Harris is leading the ridiculously early polls, with a quarter of the Democratic vote. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP There’s just one problem. Her husband, the Wall Street Journal reports, has privately told people he doesn’t want her to run. How’s that for a vote of confidence? So bite your nails, everyone. The fate of the free world, both sides are warning, hangs in the balance.
news.summary: The 2026 midterm elections are heating up as Republicans and Democrats battle for control of Congress. From Texas and Maine to Michigan, key Senate races, shifting polls and campaign spending battles add to the uncertainty, while both parties look ahead to the 2028 presidential race.

news.title: Emerging star: Why Jon Ossoff is at forefront of Democrat candidates for president
news.text:
Consigned to drift through the afterlife of boxing notoriety, former heavyweight champion Mike Tyson showed up at a Donald Trump rally in Syracuse, New York, on Friday offering a bashful wave and meaningless praise in his familiar soft lisp.

“There’s no way in the world I would ever be here if it wasn’t for a president like Donald Trump,” Tyson said.

“Ah, I watched him get in the ring so many times. He was a scary guy,” Trump said, watching as Iron Mike left the stage with his pit-pull steps. The pair are both New Yorkers and go back decades. Who knows how closely Tyson follows the US political scene but if he caught any of the midterm senate debates that aired during the week, one brawl would have caught his eye. The toss-up states of Michigan, Georgia and Texas have been defined by personality-driven contests that are openly hostile and filled with barbed accusation.

But it was the relentless and almost cruel verbal pummelling of Republican candidate Mike Collins by Georgia senator Jon Ossoff that delivered a series of swift, pulverising blows that Tyson might have recognised. For over 40 minutes, Ossoff stood beside his opponent on the stage and repeatedly called him a “bigot” before delivering an argument that was so deliberately paced and sustained that it almost became uncomfortable.

“Georgia has voter ID and that’s good. Mike Collins and Donald Trump? They’re still obsessed with turning over the 2020 election. Mike Collins still believes the 2020 election was stolen. Mike Collins has supported Donald Trump’s effort to overturn the election and he wants to give your tax dollars to the violent thugs and criminals who sacked the US Capitol on January 6th. 

“Mike Collins is attacking your voting rights. But that’s not a surprise when you consider who Mike Collins is. This is a man who cheered on a group of young men who were mocking a black woman on a college campus with monkey sounds. If John Lewis were marching today from Selma to Montgomery, Mike Collins would be grabbing a billy-club.”

The boxing ring would have at least held the mercy of a white towel. Given Georgia’s complex racial history – cradle of the civil rights movement, as Ossoff contended, yes- but also birthplace, at Stone Mountain, of the 20th-century iteration of the Ku Klux Klan, there was something shocking about the charge. 

It was the latest in Ossoff’s knack for delivering a succinct, quotable line that has seen him move, over the course of four months, from the periphery to the forefront of predictions on Democratic presidential candidates.

A day after the debate, it was announced that Trump would visit Georgia at least twice before the November 3rd midterm elections to campaign for the flailing Collins campaign. While other Republican aspirants – including Georgia gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson – are campaigning without mentioning the president’s name, Mike Collins is tethered to Trump. 

If Collins is to flip the seat that Ossoff holds – a seat essential to Democrats’ ambitions to take control of the House – then it will be as an ever-Trumper. In a television interview he gave hours after Wednesday night’s debate, Ossoff said that Collins championing Trump was predictable.

“No, I wasn’t surprised because bless his heart, Mike doesn’t have too much of a mind of his own,” he told Jen Psaki.

“He’s been doing the president’s bidding thoughtlessly now for a year and a half,” Ossoff said, before sliding into campaign mode, reminding viewers of high prices, spiralling healthcare costs, coffee up 30 per cent, ground beef up 30 per cent.

In mid-September, a Quantus Insights poll had Ossoff leading Collins by four points. This week, a series of polls has the Democrat opening up anything from an eight- to 11-point lead. It was reported that the Republicans had begun to reduce their television advertisement bookings within the state. Ossoff has amassed a formidable campaign war chest, with some $40 million available from a total campaign fund of twice that. 

Trump’s appearance in Georgia, along with his renewed pledge for $5,000 for every American voter should the Republicans hold the balance of power, will reposition the senate race as a de facto vote between the president himself and the emergent prosecutorial star of the Democratic Party.

Georgia is the state that will torment Trump after he leaves office. Although he defeated Kamala Harris there two years ago, he continues to brood over the 2020 election loss to Joe Biden by fewer than 12,000 votes, leading to his infamous phone call to Georgia’s secretary of state demanding that he “find” votes. 

Now Ossoff, considered a vulnerable re-election prospect when Trump returned to office on a wave of Maga ebullience in January 2025, has emerged as a chief thorn in his side, merciless not only in his coursing of his opponent in the Senate race, but also of Trump himself.

In flightier moments, Ossoff has drawn comparison to the late JFK – mainly for his youth and preppy-conservative wardrobe. If he possesses, within his performative repertoire, his version of Kennedy’s regal sunniness or Obama’s folksy turns, the Georgia senator is keeping it under wraps. 

For the moment, Ossoff’s message has been delivered with a steely, sombre gravity to reflect the prevailing mood. He is presenting himself as an antidote to what he would present as the frivolity and unseriousness of the Trump administration.

Having finished with his immediate opponent in the debate, he offered equally sharp appraisals of leading figures within Trump’s administration. On Pete Hegseth’s announcement that the execution of Nidal Hassan, who killed 13 people in a 2009 shooting rampage at Fort Hood, would be publicly livestreamed, Ossoff said: “I think Pete Hegseth is, frankly, a deeply unwell person who seems to relish this kind of brutality. All the while he is running a department that is falling into chaos. The guy cannot run the United States military competently and is spending his time on this obscene medieval spectacle.”

Critiquing Marco Rubio’s address in Athens, he described it as an attempt “to try and soft launch his presidential campaign”.

“These people are not focused. JD Vance and Marco Rubio are already looking past Donald Trump, jockeying for position in the future Republican primary while the administration’s obscene policies failures have made the world and our country less safe and are immiserating the American public in a cost-of-living crisis.”

Ossoff dismissed the idea of running in the 2028 election back in April but his profile has begun to fill the political sky since then. If the polling numbers alchemise into a comprehensive victory, then the speculation about his future will intensify.

For now, he remains locked into a riveting and ugly regional election framed not just by the prevailing cost-of-living issues but the spectres of race and white supremacy. This week’s debate was preceded by a report in The Daily Beast, amplified by Ossoff, that two of Collins’s campaign leaders have ties to American Patriots USA, founded by Chester Doles, a former Ku Klux Klan leader.

It’s an unpromising scenario for Trump as he prepares to visit the Peach State.

“I think the last thing that Georgia Republicans want right now is for Donald Trump to come to Georgia,” Ossoff said of that visit. “If he wants to come to Georgia, that’s fine with me.”

Early voting begins in Georgia on Tuesday.
news.summary: Georgia senator verbally pummeled his ‘bigot’ Republican rival in recent debate and has become a chief thorn in Trump’s side ahead of midterms
news.author: Keith Duggan

news.title: James Talarico’s Political Reversals Stir Trouble in Texas Senate Race
news.text:
The senate campaign of Texas Democrat James Talarico has taken some puzzling turns in recent weeks, and he has finally reappeared after a nearly two-week absence. Perhaps more information will come out soon about the nature of his illness and where he convalesced. The lack of any personal statements from Mr. Talarico during the time he was missing, along with the campaign confusion and messaging problems, indicate that the Talarico campaign may be in crisis mode.

There is another sign that the Talarico campaign is in crisis mode — shortly before his disappearance Mr. Talarico embraced the “Trust me, I’m lying” strategy regarding several of his previous radical positions, trying to temporarily position himself in the mainstream on issues such as sex-change surgery for minors and allowing “trans women” (e.g. men) to participate in women’s sports. This is a fraught strategy that rarely works any longer. It comes across as pandering dishonesty to the moderates he is appealing to, while it is simultaneously received as betrayal by activists who will not tolerate political dissimulation, even if it’s ultimately in service to their woke agenda.

In a Fox News interview in September, Mr. Talarico tried to distance himself from his previously documented statements that he now says “missed the mark.” Among these, he now claims that he:

Would “absolutely” vote for a national ban on gender surgeries for minors.Opposes trans athletes from competing in women’s sports if it endangers safety or fairness.Admits that he was wrong about there being more than two genders, and that there certainly aren’t six genders as he previously asserted.

Talarico’s problem is that he doesn’t just have a record of making outrageously woke statements, he has an actual legislative record that gives lie to his statements to Fox News. As a Texas state representative from Austin, Talarico voted against a 2023 bill which would have banned gender surgeries and puberty blockers for children. In 2021 he voted against legislation that required students to compete in athletics based on the biological sex listed on their birth certificates. Both became law, despite Talarico’s opposition. Now he is pretending that he supports those laws that he voted against.

Many of Talarico’s supporters are feeling betrayed. A Mediate piece titled “Trans Advocates Slam James Talarico for Flip-Flopping on Trans Views” quoted several angry Texas voters who are reconsidering their support for Talarico. While there is no chance that they will vote for Paxton, they might withhold their vote from Talarico. Emily Oswin-Welborn was quoted as saying “I feel like I can’t in good conscience be responsible for putting a Democrat in office that is willing to compromise on trans rights.” That is the risk of attempting the “Trust me, I’m lying” tactic with uncompromising true believers.

A pastor at Talarico’s heretical Presbyterian church, Babs Miller, expressed her disappointment about Talarico walking back support for the core tenets of the trans ideology, stating that she felt that his Democratic Party campaign team was giving him bad advice. However, she also acknowledged that Mr. Talarico was lying, stating that “I can guarantee you that once he gets elected, he’ll change his tune back to where he was.”

Despite the dubious polls showing Talarico leading Paxton in the Senate race, it will take a near-perfect confluence of events for Talarico to eke out a victory. Disregarding the historic Democrat bias of the polls involved, Talarico would need massive Democrat turnout, including that of the party’s most loyal voters — African Americans. But black Texans are not on board with Talarico, in part because he defeated Jasmine Crockett in the primary, but also because a great many find Talarico’s trans-obsession to be repugnant.

Talarico also must somehow capture a great many crossover Republican voters — the same Texas Republicans who gave Donald Trump 1.5 million more votes than Kamala Harris received in 2024 — a 14 percent margin. There are not many Trump 2024 / Talarico 2026 voters, but that is what Talarico must have in great numbers. In addition, any Republicans who find Paxton’s character off-putting will have a hard time rallying around a political chameleon who endorses the mutilation of children while talking to his base, but lies about it to moderate Republicans.

As for the efficacy of the “Trust me, I’m lying” strategy, I watched it cause the implosion of a U.S. senate race in Tennessee. In 2018 there was an open seat due to the retirement of anti-Trump Republican Bob Corker. “Moderate” Democrat Phil Bredessen, a former governor, was running against MAGA Republican Marsha Blackburn. Polls showed the race to be neck-and-neck, and the media was euphoric about Democrats flipping the seat from red to blue, which would also indicate a red-state repudiation of President Trump.

But then the Kavanaugh Supreme Court nomination became a media firestorm. Bredesen refused to take a stand, insinuating to both sides that he would vote their way on Kavanaugh if he were currently a Senator. Blackburn voiced her support for Kavanaugh, and Bredesen couldn’t avoid taking a for-or-against stand any longer. He decided to attempt the “Trust me, I’m lying” strategy by announcing that he supported Kavanaugh’s nomination … and it blew up on him. Pretty much everyone knew he was lying, except for the Democrat base, who took his words at face value. As documented in a Politico piece titled “Volunteers Bolt Bredesen Over Kavanaugh Support,” campaign volunteers canceled phone-bank and door-knocking shifts, while also running to the media to announce their feelings of betrayal.

The Bredesen situation in 2018 closely parallels the Talarico scenario in 2026. Bredesen’s campaign collapsed, and when the votes were tallied, he was crushed by Marsha Blackburn by a margin of 55 percent to 44 percent. It is likely that the Talarico-Paxton race will have a similar outcome.
