news.title: US-Israel relationship may be irreparably damaged, former Biden official warns
news.text: Phil Gordon, who served in the Biden administration as then-vice president Kamala Harris's national security advisor, issued a stark warning in an exclusive interview with The Jerusalem Post on Sunday that Israeli-US ties have been severely damaged."It's really collapsed. There's no sugarcoating it. I think Israelis need to understand that," Gordon told the Post.Gordon believes the damage inflicted on relations between Israel and the United States in recent years may be far more enduring than many Israelis realize, potentially extending well beyond the political careers of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and US President Donald Trump."I have rarely seen a turnaround in attitudes on an issue as rapid and comprehensive," Gordon said, referring to the dramatic decline in American support for Israel over the past year."You have a whole generation of Americans," he continued. "Look at the numbers on sympathy for Israelis versus Palestinians or favorable to Israel. It's really collapsed. There's no sugarcoating it. I think Israelis need to understand that."Gordon does not rule out the possibility that the deterioration could prove permanent.Asked why he recently described the damage to the relationship as "perhaps irreparably," he explained that his choice of words was deliberate."I write perhaps because I think it's still an open question, but I also don't rule it out," he said. "The more important word is irreparably because it's honestly possible."Why Gordon is speaking out nowGordon's interview comes a day after he publicly challenged efforts by Netanyahu supporters to portray a new book and interviews by Brett McGurk, a senior Biden administration official closely involved in negotiations over the Gaza war and the Israeli hostages, as vindication of the prime minister's wartime decisions.In a post on X, Gordon argued that McGurk's account, while valuable, should not be treated as the definitive version of what happened behind the scenes."While Brett's front-row account is valuable, that doesn't mean it is definitive or its perspectives widely shared, including among former members of the Biden administration," Gordon wrote."I would say most of my former colleagues think that President Biden should have put more pressure on Israel to conduct the war differently and end it sooner," he added.Gordon also wrote that few former administration officials believed Biden's biggest mistake had been publicly distancing himself from Israel, what he described as showing "daylight" between Washington and Jerusalem.Speaking to the Post, Gordon explained why he decided to enter the debate over one of the most contentious periods in recent Israeli-American relations."Everything's charged and this is sensitive and important, which is why I thought it was important for me to weigh in with my perspective," he said.His account focuses particularly on the efforts to secure a hostage agreement during the summer of 2024, including a crucial phone conversation between Biden and Netanyahu that, Gordon says, revealed just how difficult reaching a deal would become.The July 4 call: 'We were not hearing a yes… but something closer to no'On July 4, 2024, president Joe Biden called Netanyahu at what American officials believed could be a significant turning point in the negotiations to release Israeli hostages held in Gaza.According to Gordon, Hamas had just indicated it was willing to abandon one of its central demands, creating what Washington saw as a genuine opportunity for progress.To understand the significance of that moment, Gordon traced the negotiations back to the spring of 2024.For months, Hamas had insisted that Israel commit to a permanent ceasefire before any hostages were released. Israel refused to make such a commitment.That dispute remained the main obstacle throughout May.But toward the end of that month, Gordon said Israel signaled it could accept a phased ceasefire arrangement in which a permanent ceasefire would remain the ultimate objective without requiring an immediate Israeli commitment."With clever drafting, we were able to put together the proposal that President Biden rolled out publicly on May 31," Gordon said.Under that framework, Israel would not have to commit to a permanent ceasefire during the first phase, but good-faith negotiations over the final arrangements would allow for what Gordon described as "sustainable calm."The proposal represented a breakthrough because it created a possible path toward a permanent ceasefire without requiring Israel to accept Hamas's original condition upfront.For weeks, however, Hamas did not respond.Then, around July 2, Gordon said Hamas finally agreed in principle to the framework."Hamas finally came around and sort of agreed, in principle, with the framework, including dropping its demand that a permanent ceasefire be agreed up front," he recalled."That felt to us like a significant step forward. Nobody was naive in thinking that this wouldn't be difficult."With that development, Biden called Netanyahu on July 4 to urge him to move ahead."The plan was to really urge him to take the deal," Gordon said."This has gone on far too long. The hostages had suffered far too long. There was far too much catastrophic damage, Palestinian lives lost. Humanitarian conditions were horrific."But Gordon said Netanyahu's response quickly dampened American expectations."I think we, the American side, were pretty deflated to hear Netanyahu say, 'Okay, you know, I hear you, Joe, but here are all the things that will have to happen for this to work,'" Gordon recalled.Netanyahu then began listing those requirements during the call."I could tell in that moment that we were not hearing a yes or even a yes, I can work with this, but something closer to no."According to Gordon, Netanyahu subsequently began what he described as "clarifying" Israel's position, clarifications that Washington regarded as effectively introducing additional conditions into the negotiations.Philadelphi Corridor, Gallant, and the political questionOne of the most consequential Israeli demands involved retaining military forces along the entire Philadelphi Corridor, the narrow strip of territory separating Gaza from Egypt.Gordon emphasized that Israel had not even fully controlled the corridor when the original proposals were developed."In that sense, it really was a new condition," he said.Netanyahu continued insisting on that position throughout the fall of 2024, despite objections from senior Israeli officials.Gordon specifically cited then-defense minister Yoav Gallant, who, he said, considered continued control of the entire corridor militarily unnecessary and an obstacle to reaching a deal.Another disputed condition involved an Israeli screening mechanism for Palestinians returning to northern Gaza, which would have required Israeli forces to remain in central Gaza.In his earlier X post, Gordon argued that these conditions made an agreement impossible for another six months.During that period, he wrote, nearly 9,000 additional Palestinians were killed, while more Israeli hostages died, including the six hostages executed by Hamas in August 2024.He noted that both Israeli conditions were ultimately dropped from the agreement reached in January 2025.Asked directly whether Netanyahu deliberately delayed the agreement to preserve his governing coalition, Gordon declined to judge the prime minister's motivations."I can't speak to or speculate about his motives," he said."I know there was a lot of talk that he feared that he would lose his coalition if he compromised on certain issues."Gordon acknowledged that Netanyahu might genuinely have believed that continued Israeli control of the Philadelphi Corridor was militarily necessary."He certainly articulated over and over again that total victory was the only option," Gordon said.But he added that the political implications were difficult to ignore."It also seemed to be the case that keeping his coalition together depended on rejecting that proposal, so yeah, you can draw your own conclusions."Gordon stressed that no one could know with certainty whether greater flexibility by Netanyahu would have produced an agreement during the summer of 2024.Nevertheless, he argued that Netanyahu's insistence on those conditions had a clear consequence."We do know that by digging in and taking the positions that he did, which seemed to align with his political interests, and certainly aligned with his emphasis on the need for total victory, that made any deal at that time impossible," he said.A warning for Israel: Arms conditionality is now mainstream among DemocratsFor Gordon, one of the most significant consequences of the Israel-Hamas War in the Gaza Strip is not merely the deterioration in relations between Netanyahu and the Biden administration, but a broader transformation in American political attitudes toward Israel.Positions once considered marginal in debates over US military assistance have increasingly moved into the Democratic mainstream."Arms conditionality has now gone from a kind of fringe view to a mainstream Democratic position," Gordon said.He pointed to the growing number of Democratic senators supporting measures that would condition American assistance to Israel, including legislation concerning Israel's planned development in the E1 area east of Jerusalem in the West Bank.Gordon cited a Senate proposal he said virtually all Democrats supported and that would withhold assistance over E1.Although the shift has been particularly pronounced among Democrats, Gordon emphasized that declining support for Israel is not confined to one political party."I know people are mostly focused on Democrats, and it's true there's sharper criticism of Israel among Democrats, but it exists in both parties," he said.A future Israeli government adopting different policies could begin rebuilding the relationship, Gordon argued, but reversing the damage would require a sustained effort."I think with a new Israeli government and different policies, the relationship could improve, he said."With work on both sides, maybe it can be repaired, but I don't think anybody should underestimate the challenge."Should Biden have withheld more weapons from Israel?While sharply critical of Netanyahu, Gordon does not absolve the administration in which he served of responsibility.Asked what concrete pressure Biden should have applied, he rejected the idea that Washington faced only two options: continuing military assistance without conditions or imposing a comprehensive arms embargo."We had great respect for Israel's need to defend itself against Hezbollah, against Iran," Gordon said.He noted that the threat of Iranian military action was particularly real during that period, including the ballistic missile and drone attack Iran launched against Israel in April 2024.He explained that this security threat was a major reason the Biden administration did not support broadly withholding weapons.But Gordon argued that Washington had many other available tools."There's an awful lot between doing nothing and withholding all weapons," he said."It starts with diplomatic pressure. It starts with calling out Israel and pushing it to accept these agreements. You can take diplomatic measures at the United Nations and elsewhere, and then yes, you can also start conditioning weapons."He cited the administration's decision to withhold certain 2,000-pound bombs as an example of using military assistance to signal serious disagreement with Israel's conduct of the war and its handling of the humanitarian crisis.One episode particularly demonstrated the potential effectiveness of American pressure, Gordon argued: Biden's response to the Israeli strike that killed aid workers from World Central Kitchen.According to Gordon, Biden called Netanyahu and delivered a direct warning."You will do these things on the humanitarian front, and I need to see them immediately, or US policy is going to change," Gordon recalled Biden telling Netanyahu."Israel did, and opened up further crossings, and that was an example of how US pressure could work."Gordon also pointed to the pressure McGurk and Steve Witkoff applied during negotiations over the January 2025 agreement, during the presidential transition following Trump's election victory."When Brett McGurk and Steve Witkoff were pressing the Israelis to accept the final deal in January, and Trump behind the scenes, I think that kind of pressure also worked," he said.Iran before the elections: 'A volatile and dangerous stalemate'Gordon also addressed another question now dominating discussions in Jerusalem and Washington: Could Israel or the United States resume major military operations against Iran before Israel's elections and the US midterms?He refused to offer a definitive prediction, warning instead that the current confrontation was unusually volatile."We've learned over the last two years and beyond not to exclude anything," Gordon said."The situation is extremely volatile."One of his central concerns is that both Washington and Tehran believe time is working in their favor."I'm afraid that both the United States and Iran feel that time is on their side," he said."The United States thinks that the blockade is working or squeezing Iran or the economy, but Iran feels like midterms looming and pressure on the US economy means it can resist and last longer."That competing assessment, Gordon argued, explains the current diplomatic and military impasse."That's what explains this current stalemate. But it's a volatile and dangerous stalemate."Gordon fears that the pressure campaign may produce further escalation before Tehran agrees to American demands."One is that before Iran collapses, which is sort of the goal, either capitulates or collapses, which is the goal of maximum pressure, it will lash out," he said.He cited recent Houthi attacks against Riyadh and the earlier attack on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline as examples of how regional escalation can spiral, while noting that the Houthis, rather than Iran directly, were responsible for those attacks.Gordon also offered a notable assessment of Trump's military decision-making in recent months."I would say that over the past couple of months, every time Trump has threatened it and considered it, he's backed off because he has realized that the consequences could be devastating," he said."I don't know if that will hold, but I do think it's worth keeping in mind."Gordon argued that the war has already demonstrated the danger of unintended consequences."I think this war, after six months now, has proven to be catastrophic, with all sorts of unintended consequences," he said."If Israel or the United States did decide to resume a major escalation, for reasons of Israel's election or our elections, I fear that we would just see even more unintended consequences of the tragic sort that we've been seeing for the past six months."Gordon's criticism of Trump: A year of missed opportunities in GazaToward the end of the interview, Gordon turned his criticism toward Trump's handling of Gaza during the first year of his administration.The January 2025 hostage and ceasefire agreement, Gordon argued, had created an opportunity to put Gaza on a different trajectory: bring home the remaining hostages, preserve the ceasefire, establish a new governing arrangement, and begin reconstruction for Palestinians.Instead, he said, that opportunity was squandered."Once we finally got the deal in January 2025, that was an opportunity to at least start putting it on the right path, get all the hostages out, have a ceasefire, a different government in Gaza, and rebuild for Palestinians," Gordon said."But instead, Israel broke the ceasefire in March. Trump did nothing about that," he argued.According to Gordon, a complete blockade on food, water, and medicine followed for two months, dramatically worsening an already severe humanitarian crisis.He contended that Trump did not begin applying serious pressure for a renewed ceasefire until after Israel struck Doha later that year."Trump sometimes gets credit for getting the ceasefire and the 20-point plan in place, and give him credit for that, fine," Gordon said."I think it's obviously a good thing that the ceasefire was achieved, and there's a path forward in Gaza."But he argued that the administration's earlier inaction should not be forgotten."People shouldn't forget that it took a year, including turning a blind eye to a complete blockade of Gaza that severely deteriorated the humanitarian situation, and then the entire summer before he got motivated," Gordon said."And that was again only after Israel struck in Doha."For Gordon, the criticism of Netanyahu, Biden and Trump is part of the same broader argument: The Gaza war presented extraordinarily difficult choices, but he believes opportunities to end the fighting and secure the release of hostages were repeatedly missed.Now, he warns, Israel faces another formidable challenge: Rebuilding the trust and standing it has lost among the American public."With work on both sides, maybe it can be repaired," Gordon said."But I don't think anybody should underestimate the challenge."

news.title: Rep. Jeffries says Democrats are "on the verge of taking back control"
news.text: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries expressed growing confidence that his party will regain control of the House in November, as he visited two battleground districts in recent days to help Democratic candidates unseat Republican incumbents.Jeffries campaigned Friday in New Jersey's competitive 7th Congressional District alongside Democratic challenger Rebecca Bennett, a Navy veteran seeking to unseat Republican Rep. Tom Kean Jr. The following day, he traveled to Pennsylvania's 1st Congressional District to rally with Democrat Bob Harvie, a Bucks County commissioner challenging Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick.The two districts are heavily suburban, fairly affluent and politically divided — and they've caused heartburn for Democrats in recent years. The moderate Fitzpatrick has a long history of outrunning other Republicans and winning crossover support since he was first elected in 2016. Control of Kean's seat has flipped twice since 2018, but he narrowly won a competitive reelection two years ago.Democrats have invested in both races this year and view both of them as highly competitive, as they hope to take advantage of an unfavorable political environment for President Trump's party."We're running through the finish line. We take nothing for granted, but we're on the verge of taking back control of the House of Representatives," Jeffries told reporters following Saturday's event in Pennsylvania.In a briefing with a small group of political reporters Wednesday, Jeffries pointed to a handful of districts in Pennsylvania, New Jersey and New York as opportunities for Democrats. He also said he plans to visit two South Texas districts.Republicans control the House by a single-digit margin, so the outcome of the midterms could be decided by a fairly small number of races. Jeffries declined to predict how many seats his party could gain in November."I'm very confident that we're going to take back the majority, but it remains to be seen what that looks like in terms of the number of seats that we pick up, which is going to depend on the conditions that exist over the next few weeks," he said in the briefing.During the rally in Bucks County, a perennial swing county that supported Mr. Trump by a razor-thin margin in 2024 after years of narrow Democratic victories, Harvie said: "It is not an accident that Hakeem Jeffries is here tonight.""He knows what we're going to do with this district. He knows the potential," he said.Fitzpatrick's campaign told CBS News that the Republican lawmaker "is aware of Hakeem's visit, he still considers him a friend, and he looks forward to working with him in a bipartisan manner in the 120th Congress.""Leader Jeffries is doing what he needs to do, and Brian completely understands that," the campaign's statement continued.Fitzpatrick, who is seeking a sixth term, has cultivated a moderate image and put distance between himself and Mr. Trump, voting with House Democrats to rescind tariffs on Canada and restrict the Iran war. He also voted against final passage of the Trump administration's signature "Big, Beautiful Bill" last year. Most recently, he pushed back last week on the president's plan to buy diesel from Russia.Democrats have argued Fitzpatrick hasn't consistently opposed the president's agenda, pointing to an earlier vote in favor of the "Big, Beautiful Bill." Fitzpatrick has said he voted against the final legislation after the Senate added steeper Medicaid cuts.Judi Reiss, a Democratic local elected official in Lower Makefield Township, Pennsylvania, told CBS News at Saturday's rally with Jeffries and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro that she has "no personal animosity toward [Fitzpatrick] whatsoever, but he hasn't done anything. He's been a rubber stamp for Donald Trump.""He has not been independent, and it's very disappointing," said Reiss, who sought the 2020 Democratic nomination for Fitzpatrick's seat but dropped out before the primary.Still, Fitzpatrick has survived on challenging terrain in the past — and overperformed other Republicans. Vice President Kamala Harris narrowly won his district in 2024, but Fitzpatrick won reelection the same year by a more than 12-point margin.The Cook Political Report rated the Pennsylvania district "Leans Republican" on Friday, down from its previous "Likely Republican" assessment.Bucks County resident Bill Craig, a Republican who plans to vote for Fitzpatrick, told CBS News he believes Harvie has a "slim chance" of winning the district, but he expects the race to be close due to heavy Democratic turnout."Brian Fitzpatrick could cure cancer right now, and they still wouldn't vote for them," Craig said. "He's very middle-of-the-road. They're trying to paint him as some kind of MAGA psycho."Jeffries visited Fitzpatrick's district a day after campaigning for Bennett across the Delaware River, in a New Jersey seat that the Cook Political report sees as Democratic-leaning — a shift after it called the race a toss-up as recently as last month.The GOP incumbent there, Kean, is seeking a third term representing a district that stretches from the New York City suburbs to the Pennsylvania border, with Mr. Trump's Bedminster golf club sitting in the middle. He was first elected after the district was made slightly redder in 2022, and defeated Democratic Rep. Tom Malinowski.House Speaker Mike Johnson also campaigned with Kean in recent weeks.Jeffries' campaign stops illustrate the importance of suburban congressional districts that could help determine which party controls the House next year.In last week's briefing with reporters, the Democratic leader described all four competitive Republican-held districts in Pennsylvania as Democratic pickup opportunities. In addition to Fitzpatrick's seat, Democrats are targeting a northeastern Pennsylvania district and two seats in eastern and central Pennsylvania.He also singled out the race in New York's 17th Congressional District, where Democrat Cait Conley is challenging Republican Rep. Mike Lawler.Jeffries to campaign in South Texas racesMeanwhile, Democrats are defending two competitive districts in South Texas, and have signaled they plan to go on offense in two GOP-held districts in the region. Republicans made substantial gains among Latinos in 2024, especially in South Texas, where some counties that were once Democratic strongholds became light-red.Jeffries argued that Latino voters could swing back to Democrats, pointing to concerns over the cost of living and the Trump administration's aggressive immigration policies.He said the political environment has changed dramatically in the Rio Grande Valley, where Democratic Reps. Henry Cuellar and Vicente Gonzalez are seeking reelection. Jeffries said he also plans to campaign in the coming weeks for two Texas Democrats who hope to unseat Republicans. Tejano music star Bobby Pulido is running against Republican Rep. Monica De La Cruz in a toss-up district, and Democrat Johnny Garcia is challenging Republican nominee Carlos De La Cruz in a seat that's viewed as redder.The Democratic leader also rejected the notion that newly drawn Republican congressional maps in Texas and Florida would deliver the substantial gains GOP strategists had initially anticipated."Under no circumstances are Republicans winning five seats in Texas or four seats in Florida," Jeffries told CBS News last week.The National Republican Congressional Committee has disputed Democrats' increasingly optimistic assessments of the battleground map, pointing to Republican campaign resources and ground game efforts in competitive districts.If Democrats regain control of the House, Jeffries would be positioned to become the first Black speaker of the House in American history.While the party that doesn't control the White House almost always performs well in the midterms, the exact result is tougher to predict. In the 2022 midterms, when Republicans were buoyed by former President Joe Biden's unpopularity, predictions of a sweeping GOP wave failed to materialize. Republicans narrowly won control of the House but failed to recapture the Senate until two years later.Asked by CBS News whether Democrats risk that kind of election night disappointment, Jeffries acknowledged the outcome will depend on the political climate and spending.He said that while the current environment appears favorable to Democrats, the amount of money being spent by Republican-aligned political groups could ultimately limit the number of seats his party gains.House Republicans' campaign committee had more cash on hand than the group's Democratic counterpart at the end of August. Jeffries disputed suggestions that Republicans hold an overwhelming financial advantage in House battlegrounds, arguing that Democrats are effectively at parity when spending by candidates, committees and outside groups is considered together.On the GOP side, Johnson is also barnstorming frontline districts as Republicans fight to maintain their majority — and look for opportunities to unseat vulnerable Democrats. Johnson said the other day he expects to visit about 40 districts this month.In recent days, Johnson has visited Michigan and Pennsylvania with incumbent Republicans, and campaigned alongside two Iowa Republicans who are aiming to retain GOP-held districts: Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Joe Mitchell.He also campaigned last week in Ohio with Derek Merrin, who is hoping to unseat longtime Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur in a toss-up district. It's a rematch of 2024, when Merrin lost to Kaptur by around 2,400 votes.During his visit to Ohio, Johnson said he expects control of the House to be determined by at least 22 seats that he sees as "jump-balls." He has expressed optimism that Republicans can retain their majority."This will come down to the outcome of about 22 districts around the country, and I believe we can win those," Johnson told reporters late last month.Mr. Trump has also continued an aggressive campaign schedule aimed at boosting Republican candidates. Jeffries said he welcomes his increased involvement."The more Donald Trump campaigns for Republicans across the country, the better for the opportunity for Democrats to further convince the American people that we actually are the only ones determined to make life more affordable for them," Jeffries said.
news.summary: Jeffries campaigned in New Jersey and Pennsylvania and plans to campaign in Texas in the coming days to help Democratic candidates unseat Republican incumbents.
news.author: Joe Walsh

news.title: Adam Hamilton Responds After JD Vance Questions His Christianity
news.text: Democratic Kansas Senate candidate Adam Hamilton accused Vice President JD Vance of attacking his faith and spreading falsehoods about his religious beliefs, as Republicans battle to protect a seat they have held for more than a century in what has become one of the most closely watched races of the 2026 midterm elections. Hamilton, the pastor of the Church of the Resurrection, the nation's largest United Methodist congregation, responded during an interview that aired Sunday on ABC's This Week after Vance questioned his Christian beliefs and accused him of holding views that were inconsistent with Christianity. During the interview, host Jonathan Karl referenced remarks in which Vance said Hamilton believed "it's a sin to be white and a sin to raise cattle and eat meat." "I thought it was a sign of desperation," Hamilton said. "It was pathetic. He doesn't know me. Doesn't know anything about my faith." The clash comes as Democrats look to pull off a historic upset in Kansas. Republicans have held the Senate seat continuously since 1919, and no Democrat has won a Kansas Senate election since George McGill's reelection in 1932. Yet recent polling has suggested the race between Republican Senator Roger Marshall and Hamilton is effectively tied, prompting national Republicans to devote increasing attention to Kansas, a state President Donald Trump carried by more than 16 points in 2024. Hamilton has emerged as an unconventional Democratic challenger. A longtime pastor and author of more than 30 books on Christianity and theology, he has campaigned as a centrist focused on affordability, energy costs, healthcare and agriculture while seeking support from independents and moderate Republicans. Newsweek reached out to Vance, Marshall, and Hamilton on Sunday for comments. Hamilton Pushes Back on Vance's Remarks During the interview, Karl asked Hamilton about remarks Vance made during a September 14 campaign stop in Olathe, Kansas, while campaigning for Marshall. Hamilton said he was surprised by the attack. "The vice president of the United States would come here and attack the faith of a pastor of the largest church in the state of Kansas, the largest United Methodist church in the country," he said. Hamilton pointed to his decades in ministry and challenged Vance's characterization of his beliefs. "I wake up every morning. I slip to my knees. I offer my life to Christ. I pray for the Holy Spirit to lead me. I read scripture. I carry the Bible with me everywhere I go," he said. At one point, Hamilton added: "Let's compare theology. Let's compare our faith and the impact we're having on the world." 'Every Single Line...Was a Lie' Karl also cited comments in which Vance accused Hamilton of holding views that he argued were inconsistent with Christianity. According to the remarks read on-air, Vance said Hamilton believes "it's a sin to be white and a sin to raise cattle and eat meat." Hamilton flatly rejected the accusation. "Every single line of what you just read was a lie," he said. "There was no part of what he said was true." Hamilton said the criticism stemmed from a sermon discussing racism and the Christian concept of repentance. "I never talked about repenting for being white. You can't find that in anything I've ever said. Or repenting for eating beef," he said. He argued the controversy reflected broader problems in the country's political discourse. "That's what's wrong with our country today, with our politics, with what's happening in Washington, D.C.," Hamilton said. A Different Kind of Kansas Democrat The exchange highlights why Republicans have targeted Hamilton so aggressively in recent weeks. Marshall and his allies have attempted to portray Hamilton as a liberal Democrat out of step with Kansas voters. Marshall has previously described him as "too woke for Kansas," while Republicans have argued his sermons mirror the national Democratic Party's priorities. Hamilton has instead tried to present himself as a faith-based moderate. During the ABC interview, he emphasized that he spent much of his life as a Republican and said he has supported candidates from both parties. In a recent Politico interview, Hamilton described himself as "an independent-minded Democrat." "I'm standing in the center, and it's the extremes that seem to be trying to pull us apart," he said. "But I think there's far more of us who stand in the center saying, look, we've got to work together." Hamilton's balancing act reflects a broader challenge facing Democrats in red states. Earlier this month, Hamilton suggested former Vice President Kamala Harris should keep her distance from the Kansas race, arguing her involvement could undermine his ability to win over crossover voters in a state Trump carried comfortably in 2024. The comment underscored Hamilton's effort to position himself as an independent-minded candidate rather than a standard national Democrat, a theme he returned to repeatedly during Sunday's interview. Hamilton said he had been both a Republican and a Democrat during his adult life and argued that voters were looking for leaders focused on competence and character rather than party labels. "What matters to me more than the letter behind your name is who you are, what you stand for, your character," he said. Why Kansas Matters The increasingly heated rhetoric underscores growing Republican concerns about a race that, until recently, was not expected to be competitive. National forecasters have steadily moved Kansas closer to battleground status as Democrats seek the four-seat net gain needed to retake control of the Senate. Concerns about inflation, diesel and fertilizer costs, the war in Iran and Trump's approval ratings have helped put pressure on Republicans in several red and red-leaning states. Hamilton has particularly focused on economic frustrations among farmers and rural communities, arguing that Republicans have failed to address rising costs. During his interview with ABC, he said many Kansans who supported Trump now feel Washington is not listening to them. "We need a senator who's going to say, Mr. President, this is not good for my people," Hamilton said. Whether that message is enough to break one of the longest Senate winning streaks in American politics remains to be seen. But with just weeks remaining until Election Day, both parties increasingly view Kansas as a race worth watching.
news.summary: Adam Hamilton pushes back after JD Vance questions his Christianity in Kansas' tightening Senate race.
news.author: Steve Mollman

news.title: Revealed: How unknown donors with South Asian and Middle Eastern backgrounds are spending millions funding the rise of the far-Left... as they plot to dominate midterm elections
news.text:
A series of practically unknown wealthy individuals with little history of political spending have been donating millions of dollars to support far-Left candidates in the 2026 midterm elections. 

Progressives have been scooping up primaries across the US over the past few months with the support of far-Left organizations such as the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), and funding from Democratic establishment and 'anti-Aipac' super PACs.

The money flowing into those races has come in large part from non-traditional donors, many of whom are of South Asian or Middle Eastern descent and work in industries such as tech and medicine. 

The top-two donors to the most popular 'anti-Aipac' super PAC, American Priorities, are Mohammad Waqas and Omer Hassan, who are both executives at tech companies.

The single largest donor to progressive causes this election cycle, Saikat Chakrabarti, has given a total of $13.4 million to various campaigns and PACs. Chakrabarti earned his fortune through early equity in the tech company Stripe as one of its first software engineers.

American Priorities' top-12 donors have collectively given the group around $5.7 million during the 2025 to 2026 election cycle, according to Federal Election Commission filings reviewed by the Wall Street Journal.

Among those 12, four had given no money to the PAC between 2014 and 2024, including the two highest donors who together gave $2.1 million over the past year. 

The rest donated just a fraction of what they spent over the past year between 2014 and 2024. Five of the top-12 donors also gave to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's campaign. None of those five live in New York.

The new class of non-traditional donors have helped spur a projected blue wave in the 2026 midterms, as polling indicates that Democrats are likely to take control of the House of Representatives and potentially the Senate as well. 

Political analyst Nate Silver, who has accurately predicted the outcome of many presidential elections, gave Democrats a 93 percent chance of winning the House and 75 percent chance of winning the Senate. 

The prediction market Polymarket has pegged the odds of a House takeover at 91 to 93 percent and a Senate takeover at 64 percent. 

Progressive candidates are showing polling advantages over their Republican counterparts in races across the country, and some races in previously solid-red districts are coming down to a tossup. 

Abdul El-Sayed, who has former connections to DSA but says he is not affiliated with the organization, has been endorsed by Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Kamala Harris in his race to win a Senate seat in Michigan. 

Polls predict that the election is leaning in his favor as he faces off against Republican opponent Mike Rogers. 

The race between progressive candidate Randy Villegas and Republican incumbent David Valadao for California House Seat 22 has come down to a tossup, despite Valadao winning his seat by nearly seven points two years ago. 

The race between progressive candidate Brian Poindexter and Republican incumbent Max Miller for Ohio House Seat 7 has also come down to a tossup, despite the district not having elected a Democrat to the US House since 1936.

Those races are just a few examples of a larger story playing out across the nation this election cycle.

news.title: Jon Ossoff Extends Lead Over Mike Collins in Georgia Senate Race Poll
news.text: Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff has extended his lead over his Republican challenger, Representative Mike Collins, according to a new poll of the Georgia Senate race. The Trafalgar Group’s latest poll found Ossoff is leading Collins by 8 percentage points, 51 percent to 43 percent, with 5.9 percent of respondents saying they were undecided. The poll was conducted between October 7 and 9 among 1,101 likely general election voters and has a margin of error of plus or minus 2.9 percentage points. The findings represent a modest improvement for Ossoff from the polling firm’s September poll, which gave him a six-point lead. That poll, conducted between September 10 and 12 among 1,091 likely voters, found Ossoff had 49.4 percent support, while Collins had 42.8 percent support. That poll found 1.3 percent said they would vote for Libertarian candidate Allen Buckley, while 6.5 percent were still undecided. That poll also had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.9 percentage points. Trafalgar was founded by Robert Cahaly, who has served as a political consultant for Republicans, and is generally seen as having a Republican lean. The firm has overestimated Republicans in some races, particularly in 2022, but also correctly predicted President Donald Trump’s victory in 2016 even as many other pollsters forecasted that Democratic candidate Hillary Clinton held an advantage. Georgia's Senate race remains one of the most closely watched contests of the midterms. Republicans believe the race is competitive, pointing to Trump’s 2-point victory over former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024. But Democrats believe that Trump’s national approval rating, which has declined amid economic concerns, could give them an advantage in the closely divided swing state. Although Georgia backed Trump in 2024, former President Joe Biden won it in 2020, and it reelected Democratic Senator Raphael Warnock in 2022. Growth around the blue-shifting Atlanta metro has turned the once-Republican state into a battleground, and Democrats hope those trends will continue to boost Ossoff this year. Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority in the Senate, with Democrats needing to flip four seats as well as defend all of the seats they currently hold, including in Georgia, to win a majority. The Cook Political Report rates the races as Likely Democrat, while RealClearPolling rates it as Leans Democrat. Newsweek has contacted the Ossoff and Collins campaigns for comment via email. Ossoff Faces Off With Collins in Debate During a debate on Thursday, Ossoff and Collins clashed over key issues. Affordability was a major topic, with voters consistently citing it among their top concerns in this year’s midterms. During the debate, Ossoff repeatedly asked Collins to justify his support for Trump’s tariff policies, which he said have “crushed Georgia families.” Ossoff said he would repeal the tariffs and also pointed to the ongoing war in Iran that is contributing to the soaring price of gasoline. Collins blamed inflation on Biden administration policies. When asked about his plan to make life more affordable for Georgians, he said he wants to continue to be energy independent and export goods out of the port in Savannah. What Other Polls Show A recent Wedgewood Poll survey shows Ossoff with 55 percent of the potential vote compared to 45 percent for Collins. The poll surveyed 600 likely voters on October 2- 3 and has a 4 percent margin of error. A Big Data Poll similarly shows Ossoff leading Collins, with 51 percent to 40.1 percent among registered voters and 52.2 percent to 41.0 percent among likely voters. The poll surveyed 712 registered voters and 678 likely voters in the Peach State from September 21-23. The margin of error was 4 percent. A Quantus Insights poll shows Ossoff with 48.2 percent compared to Collins' 44.4 percent, while 6.5 percent are undecided and 0.9 percent said they prefer someone else. The poll surveyed 645 likely voters from September 14-16 and had a margin of error of 4.3 percent. Rival prediction market Polymarket also favors Ossoff. His odds of winning have increased on the platform over the midterms cycle, with a 96 percent chance as of Sunday. Collins has a 4 percent chance on the platform. Prices fluctuate as traders react to polling, fundraising, candidate developments and broader political trends. They measure trader sentiment at a given moment but do not always accurately predict the future. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. news.summary: Georgia's Senate race remains one of the most closely watched contests of this year's midterms.

news.title: Pollsters Reveal Why Dems’ Blue Wave Isn’t a Sure Thing
news.text:
Democrats’ dreams of a blue wave could be inflated by the voters pollsters can’t reach, experts warn.

Inaccurate sample groups, skewed data sampling, and unknowable voter behavior can all affect the outcome of a poll and could be inflating support for the Democrats, pollsters said.

Poll after poll has painted a disastrous picture ofr Republicans—who could lose Senate seats in deep red states like Texas and House races in red districts all over America. 

In Texas, Democrat James Talarico is polling ahead of Trump-backed Republican Ken Paxton, fueling hopes of flipping a Senate seat in the longtime GOP stronghold.

Democrats lead Republicans in the RealClearPolling generic congressional average by almost 8 percentage points. 

Some surveys have them ahead by up to 16 points. But the size of that lead depends in part on how pollsters assemble their samples and identify likely voters.

Republican voters are increasingly difficult to reach for voter surveys. To compensate, pollsters are giving greater weight to GOP voters who do respond, but those respondents may not represent the Republicans who are not being captured in surveys.

“The adjustment assumes that the Republicans who respond to a poll are similar to the Republicans who don’t respond to the poll,” Rice University political science assistant professor Matthew Tyler told Axios.

Trump voters have been the hardest to predict, with polling in 2016, 2020, and 2024 all underestimating the octogenarian president’s base. 

Republican pollster and founder of Cygnal, Brent Buchanan, told Axios Kamala Harris’s base was more willing to be surveyed, but that shouldn’t stop pollsters from getting the correct results. 

“We definitely have more people answering surveys who voted for Harris than who voted for President Trump, but if you’re a good pollster, you still get the other people.”

In a blog post this week YouGov chief scientist Doug Rivers broke down the volatility of the survey process, and explained how who is included in the survey can drastically change its outcome. 

He modeled several scenarios, including one with the Democrats leading by 6 points, the other with them ahead 16. The difference? The group of likely voters they used to create the results. 

The discrepancy, Rivers noted, was “roughly the difference between a gentle swell and a tsunami.”

Donald Trump, however, continues to insist neither scenario is accurate. In the face of terrible poll after terrible poll, the president has maintained that his party will win the midterms. 

As his own approval slumps to new lows and Americans are squeezed by the cost of living and surging gas prices thanks to Trump’s Iran war, he has rejected every poll as “fake news.”

Still, the possibility there could be an unrecorded mass of Trump voters waiting in the wings to save the day for the GOP is unlikely, Buchanan notes. 

“I think it’s telling that we’re hanging our hopes on, ‘The polls are wrong.’ That’s not very strong.”

The White House and the Democratic National Committee did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

news.title: Trump’s BBC lawsuit backfires spectacularly as judge drags his children into £7.5billion legal nightmare
news.text: Donald Trump’s attempt to bully the BBC into submission has backfired spectacularly after a US judge cleared the way for his own children to be dragged into his £7.5billion defamation battle. In a humiliating setback for the US President, his eldest son, Donald Trump Jr, daughter Ivanka and son-in-law Jared Kushner now face subpoenas demanding documents and testimony about the events surrounding the January 6 Capitol riots. They are to be called by BBC lawyers after Trump sued the corporation for billions of dollars over an episode of Panorama detailing the January 6 riots. It is a devastating twist in a lawsuit Trump launched, expecting to put the broadcaster on the defensive, after watching some of America’s biggest media organisations hand over millions to settle legal disputes with him. The BBC has refused to roll over. To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed. An insider told the Mirror : “Whereas Trump and his team thought the BBC would roll over much as US TV bosses have, nothing could be further from the truth. They are fighting it all the way. "Not only is he on the hook for a subpoena, but now his kids and Kushner are too. Trump has tried to amend his claims against the corporation to limit the scope of what information they can access, but after opening up a can of worms, he has failed miserably to put the top back. This case is running away from the president at an alarming rate.” The latest win for the BBC came on Friday, as US Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett authorised the corporation to serve subpoenas on the three members of Trump’s family via alternative methods after attempts to deliver them in person were thwarted by their security. The BBC’s attempts to physically serve Don Jr., Ivanka, and her husband, Kushner, with papers have been repeatedly blocked by the Secret Service. Now, Beeb lawyers have been told they can bypass their close protection agents, delivering the legal demands by registered mail to home and business addresses and through lawyers. The decision opens the door to Trump’s closest relatives being questioned about what they knew of his actions on January 6, 2021, when his supporters stormed the US Capitol. The three could be required to provide documents and answer questions under oath, although the ruling authorises service of the subpoenas rather than finally resolving any objections to their scope. For Trump, who has spent years fiercely protecting both his family and his business interests from scrutiny, the prospect is an extraordinary own goal. His lawyers had accused the BBC of using the subpoenas to gain politically-motivated leverage over the President, portraying the move as harassment rather than legitimate evidence-gathering. But Judge Lett rejected the procedural roadblock, accepting that conventional efforts to serve the documents had proved unsuccessful. And the trouble does not end with Trump's children. In another ruling on Friday, the judge authorised subpoenas to be served by certified mail and email on Eric Herschmann, a former Trump White House lawyer who may possess information relevant to the case. Herschmann had also proved difficult to serve despite attempts to contact him at his home and business. The BBC is now pursuing an expanding circle of people with potentially valuable knowledge of Trump’s conduct during one of the darkest episodes in modern American history. It stems from a legal action the President himself chose to launch. Trump sued the corporation over a Panorama documentary broadcast before the 2024 presidential election that misleadingly spliced together separate portions of his speech before the Capitol attack. The edit created the impression that Trump had directly connected his call for supporters to march on the Capitol with his later declaration that they should “fight like hell”. The BBC acknowledged the editing mistake, apologised and promised not to broadcast the programme again. But it rejected Trump’s demand for compensation, maintaining that the documentary did not meet the legal threshold for defamation. That refusal sets the corporation apart from American media giants that have already reached costly settlements with the President. Disney, which owns ABC News, agreed to pay £11.3 million towards Trump’s presidential library and another £750,000 in legal costs following a dispute over comments by presenter George Stephanopoulos. Paramount agreed to pay £12 million to settle his lawsuit over CBS’s editing of an interview with Kamala Harris , despite denying wrongdoing. Those settlements fuelled concerns that powerful media organisations were becoming increasingly unwilling to challenge a President notorious for using litigation against his critics. Trump’s case against the BBC is scheduled for trial in Miami in February next year.
news.summary: Donald Trump’s £7.5billion lawsuit against the BBC has backfired after a judge cleared the way for his children and son-in-law to face subpoenas and potentially give evidence under oath, as the broadcaster fights back against the President’s legal offensive.

news.title: Trump’s tariffs forced U.S. factories to close down or lay off workers, and longtime GOP voters are revolting—’It was like taking a knife to the back’
news.text:
Last year, Vandermeer’s premonition came true in a very personal way. The 62-year-old lost his job as a product designer at Howard Miller, a clockmaker that relied on parts produced overseas. After a century in business, the company in Zeeland, Michigan, closed its factory, sold off its inventory and brand name and laid off nearly 200 workers.

“So much for bringing jobs back,” Vandermeer said. Next month, he plans to vote straight Democrat in the midterms.

As if an unpopular war with Iran and persistent inflation were not enough trouble for Republicans, they are confronting a backlash over the tariffsthat Trump made a cornerstone of his economic agenda. He promised that charging higher taxes on imports would spur a factory renaissance in the United States, but that has not come to pass. Although the country has added manufacturing jobs so far this year, the sector has fewer employees than when Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.

White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers insisted that a factory boom is underway, citing increases in manufacturing output and more work in certain nonresidential construction trades. “Factory construction jobs of today mean more manufacturing jobs down the road once those factories come online,” she said.

Even before the tariffs, Howard Miller struggled as Americans lost their taste for fancy timepieces such as its signature grandfather and mantel clocks. So the company broadened its offerings years ago to include bar carts, cabinets and consoles.

But those products also depended on glass and other parts from abroad, and diversification did not ensure survival.

“I could still have a job, but now I don’t because of tariffs,” Vandermeer said. “It was like taking a knife to the back.”

Job losses pile up in battleground states

Vandermeer lives in Michigan’s 4th Congressional District, which is represented by Republican Bill Huizenga, who is running for a ninth term in the Nov. 3 election.

Before Trump implemented his broadest set of tariffs last year, on what the president called “Liberation Day,” Huizenga was supportive.

“Is it going to be easy? Not necessarily. Is it the right thing to do? Absolutely it is,” he told reporters at the time.

A spokesperson for Huizenga said last week that the congressman “sees a potential role for tariffs” for boosting domestic manufacturing “while recognizing the need to address their broader economic effects.” His Democratic opponent, state Sen. Sean McCann, has criticized the incumbent for opposing legislation that would rein in tariffs that Trump imposed unilaterally.

There are similar issues in competitive races in Kansas, Iowa and Ohio, where Republican acquiescence could hurt the party on Election Day as their constituents face factory layoffs, farm foreclosures and higher prices.

Tracy Chew, 55, voted for Trump in 2016, then for Democrat Joe Biden in 2020 and Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024.

She used to work for Case, a backhoe manufacturer, but the company announced before the tariffs that it would close its plant in Burlington, Iowa. She lost her job in April, as did her daughter, followed by husband and son-in-law over the next few weeks.

Chew is leaning toward voting for Democrats again this year, feeling that Trump let them down.

“I’m furious he isn’t doing enough,” she said. “Tariffs are not targeting the right companies, the right amount.”

Layoffs in Iowa have piled up elsewhere.

Winnebago Industries, which produces recreational vehicles like campers, cut 200 jobs last year after the cost of importing aluminum, steel and electronics increased by tens of millions of dollars.

“It’s a day to day battle,” said Michael Happe, the company’s chief executive.

In the tight race for an open U.S. Senate seat in Iowa, U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson faces Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek. There is a close contest, too, in Kansas, where Democrat Adam Hamilton, the pastor of the largest United Methodist Church in the U.S., is trying to unseat Republican Roger Marshall.

Cole Hoppock, chief executive of appliance maker Vornado Air in Wichita, Kansas, said Trump’s tariffs “impacted virtually everything.” The company known for its retro household fans laid off more than 70 factory workers in February, blaming higher prices for imported parts.

Trump’s trade policy could force cutbacks soon at another Kansas employer, Canadian jet manufacturer Bombardier. Trump has threatened to ban the company’s sales in the U.S. if Bombardier does not start making all its planes in the U.S. Bombardier said it buys parts from 2,800 companies in 47 states, including in Kansas, where it employs more than 1,000 people

Trump’s approach to trade is unpopular

Trump has spent years complaining that other countries are ripping off the U.S. when it comes to trade. Most economists say he is wrong and that his remedy — broad universal tariffs — would cause more pain than help.

Now most Americans disagree with Trump’s approach, according to The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research. A September poll showed only about 3 in 10 U.S. adults approve of Trump’s handling of trade negotiations, compared with 4 in 10 in March.

Some of Trump’s tariffs have been haphazard.

He targeted Brazil because of political differences and he jacked up tariffs on China to levels so extreme that they risked a recession and forced the president to retreat. The Supreme Court in February ruled against Trump’s declaration of an emergency to roll out his “Liberation Day” tariffs last year, leaving foreign trade unsettled as the administration continues to adjust with new levies and threats.

Tariffs are far from the only reason for the lost of manufacturing jobs, and factories have cut workers for decades with or without them. Even some Republicans who dislike Trump’s approach will not split with the party.

Bicycle Corp. of America, which closed its factory in South Carolina last year, blamed rising prices for imported parts. Koby Bird, who retired after working in quality control, likes tariffs but was frustrated by Trump’s habit of raising and lowering them seemingly at whim.

“It was all over the place,” Bird said. “Businesses couldn’t plan.”

Next month, Bird is likely to stick with Republicans, including U.S. Sen. Darline Graham, because tariffs are only one issue and he believes Democrats would spend too much money on the wrong things.

Ernie Goss, an economist at Creighton University in Nebraska, said manufacturing woes may not convert to Democratic victories. He said some people may “think the tariffs in the long run will work.”

Some workers may be turning on Trump

Wendell Young, a union leader in Pennsylvania, where several factories have had layoffs, said he senses a backlash among workers.

Last summer, Young said he got a firestorm of angry responses to his email blaming tariffs for a decision by Post Holdings to cut 160 jobs at a local pet food factory.

“Keep politics out of this,” wrote one of workers at the plant in Bloomsburg, Pennsylvania. “President Trump isn’t the reason.”

“People used to beat me up for not supporting Trump. I haven’t heard that in a year,” said Young, president of Local 1776 of the United Food and Commercial Workers International Union. “Some of these people are red Republicans and they are shocked. They expected more jobs.”

Post Holdings ultimately agreed to reduce the head count by offering severance for people to leave, but lower production had a ripple effect.

Local can manufacturer Trivium Packaging decided to cut several jobs because they were getting less orders from Post and other companies, according to Young’s union.

“I understand the mindset behind tariffs, but I just don’t know if it’s working,” said former Trivium worker Heather Kingston. She left for another company before the layoffs, and her husband is still working at Trivium. “There doesn’t seem to be many manufacturing jobs moving into the area,” she said.

Kingston said she voted for Republican Dan Meuser in the 9th District last time but is having doubts this year. Meuser’s seat is considered safe, but other races in the state are up for grabs, including in the 7th and 8th districts, which are near the Post and Trivium factories.
news.summary: “So much for bringing jobs back,” Vandermeer said. Next month, he plans to vote straight Democrat in the midterms.
news.author: Bernard Condon,The Associated Press

news.title: Midterms Appear Grim For GOP — But Michele Tafoya Within Striking Distance In Minnesota
news.text:
Republican Minnesota Senate nominee and former NBC Sports reporter Michele Tafoya is polling well in her Senate race in the blue state of Minnesota, while many Republican candidates struggle in traditionally red states. 

While Republican candidates in red states struggle to fend off their Democratic opponents, Tafoya’s opponent, Democratic Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, leads by an average of 1.6 points in a state that has not had a Republican senator since 2009, when former Republican Minnesota Sen. Norm Coleman left office. The Minnesota Republican centered her campaign around her state’s fraud scandals throughout Democratic Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz’s administration, of which Flanagan is a part. 

Tafoya’s campaign told the Daily Caller News Foundation that she is performing well compared to other Republican candidates because of her message to hold “fraudsters accountable,” which they argued has resonated with Minnesota voters. 

“Michele’s common sense message of ending fraud and holding fraudsters accountable is resonating with Minnesotans,” the Tafoya campaign told the DCNF. “During Peggy Flanagan’s eight years as lieutenant governor, billions of our tax dollars were stolen, violent gang activity increased, and test scores declined. Peggy Flanagan has already shown Minnesotans she is incapable of leadership. Next month, Minnesota voters will send her a pink slip.”

Flanagan’s campaign did not respond to the DCNF’s request for comment on whether they are concerned that the fraud scandal could cost Flanagan the election. 

RealClearPolling rated the race a “Toss Up” in September after multiple polls showed either a tie or Tafoya within the margin of error. 

Cook Political Report rated the Minnesota Senate race as “likely Democrat.” The forecaster remained skeptical that Tafoya could flip the Senate seat due to the economy and the raids conducted by Immigration and Custom Enforcement (ICE). 

“We’re skeptical of some public polling that has shown the race close, and Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan has only just now started spending after a brutal Democratic primary. Former NFL reporter Michele Tafoya has an interesting profile, and national GOP sources maintain that voters’ anger over the state’s widespread fraud scandal will stick to Flanagan. But given the economy and the state’s ICE raids, this is a difficult climate to try to make a major play in a state Kamala Harris won,” Cook Political Report wrote. 

Riots and protests broke out in Minnesota over Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) raids. Tensions escalated when two protesters, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, were killed by immigration agents. 

Former Vice President Kamala Harris won Minnesota 51.1% to 46.9%. over President Donald Trump during the 2024 presidential election.

Fraudsters, most of whom were of Somali descent, allegedly stole hundreds of millions of Minnesotans’ taxpayer dollars from state programs since 2018, such as Feeding Our Future, which provided meals for low-income children during the COVID-19 pandemic. The Department of Justice (DOJ) charged 80 suspects with stealing around $250 million from Feeding Our Future. (RELATED: 10 Times Democrats, Corporate Media Leaped To Defend Somalis Despite Massive Fraud Scandals)

Somali fraudsters allegedly stole over $90 million from Medicaid and child care programs throughout the state, including $46.6 million in autism fraud (EIDBI), $22 million in individualized home supports, and $15.7 million in housing stabilization services, according to the DOJ. 

The top priority listed on Tafoya’s campaign website is her plan to address fraud. She called for deporting any immigrant convicted of fraud in the U.S., imposing tough mandatory sentencing to ensure fraudsters serve their sentences in federal prison and strip federal funding from states that refuse to implement anti-fraud controls or follow basic audit practices, according to the website. 

Flanagan’s campaign website does not mention fraud, but calls for ending corruption, passing Medicare for All and ending Trump’s mass deportation policy. 

Affordability remained the top issue for voters throughout the 2026 midterm cycle. Minnesotans felt the pinch of the theft of their taxpayers while also paying among the highest taxes in the U.S. The state ranks 44th overall in the Tax Foundation’s state tax competitiveness index. 

TUNE IN: Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan wears a hijab while showing her support for the Somali community. "I am incredibly clear that the Somali community is part of the fabric of the state of Minnesota!" https://t.co/xunG3p8TcB— Resist the Mainstream (@ResisttheMS) December 26, 2025

Walz dropped his 2026 gubernatorial reelection bid in January after his administration received backlash over the fraud scandal. Senior Minnesota state officials allegedly hired outside investigators to silence whistleblowers in an attempt to cover up widespread state social services fraud. 

A survey from August found that 39% of Minnesotans “strongly” disapproved of Walz’s job performance as governor, while 17% strongly approved, according to KSTP Eyewitness News, an ABC News affiliate. A poll by the Star Tribune/KARE 11/ Hubbard School of Journalism and Mass Communication Minnesota found Walz had a 39% approval rating in the state in June, while 53% disapproved. 

Tafoya won four Sports Emmy Awards and covered five Super Bowls and 327 NFL games. She made her national debut at the U.S. Open Tennis Championships, and was a sideline reporter for NBC Sports’ highly-rated “Sunday Night Football” broadcasts. 

Tafoya raised $5.3 million between Jan. 1, 2025, and July 22, according to the latest Federal Election Commission (FEC) records. Since Republican PACs and committees do not typically spend large sums on candidates in blue states, her campaign received $230,000 from those groups. 

Flanagan raised over $6.5 million in that same time frame, FEC filings show. 

Tafoya and Flanagan are set to debate on Oct. 16. 

Tafoya is not the only Republican candidate to perform well in a traditionally blue state this cycle. Republican state Sen. Christine Drazan is neck-and-neck with Democratic Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek in the state’s governor’s race, despite Oregon being a blue-leaning state, according to RealClear Polling 

Republican candidates in deep red states and districts are struggling to fend off their Democratic challengers, causing Republican political action committees (PACs) to spend unprecedented amounts of money in states like Texas, Kansas and Iowa, and cut spending in battleground states like North Carolina since former Democratic North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper held a solid lead against Republican North Carolina Senate candidate Michael Whatley. 

Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton trailed Democratic Texas Senate candidate James Talarico by 2.8 points, according to RealClearPolling. In Kansas, Republican Sen. Roger Marshall was neck-and-neck with Democratic Kansas Senate candidate Adam Hamilton after reports revealed he sued 700 of his patients for outstanding medical bills during his time as an OB-GYN, The New York Times reported. 

Texas has not had a Democratic senator since 1993, while Kansas last had a Democrat senator in 1939. Republican candidates could lose to Democrats in Alaska, Iowa and Ohio.
news.summary: ‘Resonating with Minnesotans’
news.author: Nicole Silverio

news.title: Rep. Tom Kean Jr. might lose, but not because of four-month absence
news.text:
WESTFIELD, NJ – Rep. Tom Kean Jr., R-New Jersey, spent nearly four months mysteriously absent from Congress in the spring, and Washington was buzzing with speculation as to why. After his June reemergence and explanation that he had been in treatment for depression, political observers wondered if questions about his ability to do his job would harm his bid for reelection.

“No one is campaigning saying ‘Kean was hospitalized for depression and shouldn’t be re-elected’ but there is a well-established finding in political science showing that perceptions that the incumbent isn’t doing their job is just about the most powerful attack a challenger can make,” Dan Cassino, a political science professor and pollster at Fairleigh Dickinson University in New Jersey, said. 

Now, four weeks out from the Nov. 3 midterm elections, Kean's seat in the House of Representatives is one on a list of toss-up districts that Democrats seem poised to flip blue. His Democratic opponent, Rebecca Bennett, is leading Kean by five points, according to a Insider NJ/StimSight poll released Sept. 14.

But Kean's absence seems to be a small factor for voters in the New Jersey swing district, who told USA TODAY that they sympathize with their representative − even if they aren't voting for him.

More: These races will decide whether Democrats or Republicans win House control

New Jersey’s 7th Congressional District is usually a swing district 

The district − home to President Donald Trump’s Bedminster golf club − stretches from New York City suburbs to more rural parts of the state near Pennsylvania. It has been competitive in recent election cycles: Democrats held it from 2019-2023, and before that Republicans represented the district for over a decade. Kean flipped the seat back to the GOP in 2022 after the state redistricted following the 2020 Census. The new district was considered more Republican-leaning after the shift.

In 2024, Kean beat Democratic challenger Sue Altman by nearly five percentage points and Trump won the district, but Democrat Mikie Sherrill carried it in the state’s 2025 gubernatorial election.

Most voters express sympathy for Kean

Among New Jersey voters USA TODAY spoke with in affluent Westfield, historic, semi-rural Flemington Borough and the middle-to-upper class community of Somerville, the sentiment was mixed. A handful of voters said they did not know about the representative's absence from Capitol Hill and some did not even know that an election was coming up. 

One Republican woman and 30-year Flemington resident, who would not share her name, told USA TODAY that Kean's depression experience makes her want to vote for him more, because Kean could relate to something that a lot of people experience.

“Tom," a Democrat from Raritan Township who would only give his first name, said that he does think many voters are aware of Kean’s absence and shared that his wife attended a rally raising complaints about it outside the district’s congressional office in the spring. Tom said that while he does feel bad for the congressman's mental health struggles, he does not agree with Kean's voting record.

Columbus O’Berry, a U.S. Army veteran living in Somerville, said he will be “sticking with the Democratic Party,” but he expressed sympathy for Kean’s illness, telling USA TODAY that the politician is “just like anybody else, he’s human.”

Republican leadership sticks by Kean

House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-Louisiana, defended his Republican colleague throughout his spring absence, telling reporters at the time, "He's had a medical issue. I don't even know the details, and I have to respect that."

Kean's seat is one of the races that could determine whether Johnson keeps the speaker's gavel.

In August, Johnson made a campaign stop with Kean in New Jersey, telling reporters for WFMZ-TV that “when you rank the races, the closest races around the country, everyone looks to the 7th District of New Jersey almost every cycle, as a really important one.” 

Kean Jr. comes from a well-known New Jersey family that is the namesake for the state’s public research institution Kean University. His father is former Gov. Thomas Kean, who served from 1982 to 1990. His grandfather, former Rep. Robert W. Kean, served in Congress from 1939 to 1959. 

Both candidates avoid discussing Kean's absence

In a Sept. 27 debate between the candidates, Kean defended his handling of the absence saying, “nobody can plan a medical emergency and that was a medical emergency and we were very clear with our constituents as well as the press that we were seeking medical treatment.” 

“We were also very transparent when we spoke on the house floor about my condition of depression and make sure we want to get rid of the stigma associated with any mental health issues,” Kean said. 

Bennett said in a statement upon Kean’s return to Congress that she was “relieved that Congressman Tom Kean Jr. is well” and wished him good health, but also added that she “got into this race because Tom Kean Jr. was failing our community long before this absence.” 

Bennett – casually referred to as “Rebecca” by voters who spoke with USA TODAY – is a retired U.S. Navy helicopter pilot and former healthcare executive. Her campaign has stayed away from his absence and mental health, instead criticizing the incumbent for his support of Trump's tax and spending cuts and focusing on her own priorities such as affordability, which is her party's leading issue this year.

Cassino doesn’t see Kean's prolonged absence as something that will directly affect voters. He also noted that while Kean was seeking treatment, he wasn’t on the campaign trail and lost valuable time that “he could have been using to build up a stronger relationship with his constituents.” 

“Kean has been so lowkey a member of Congress, so eager to stay out of the media that his illness might be the only time voters have heard anything about him,” he said. “That’s less an effect of the illness than it is an effect of Kean’s campaign style, but it’s a problem for him.” 

Micah Rasmussen, director of the Rebovich Institute for New Jersey Politics at Rider University, noted that the most recent polling in the district didn’t ask about Kean's illness and absence, so “we don't know exactly what voters are thinking about it.” 

“Republicans were hoping it would be old news by now, and up until this week, they'd more or less gotten their wish in that the campaign had been focused mostly on other issues like health care, stock trades, and the affordability of gas and groceries,” he told USA TODAY. 

He explained that the House Majority PAC, which supports Democrats running for the House, ran two ads in late September to remind voters of Kean’s absense and that when money is spent on specific messaging like that, it has been tested and is expected to resonate with voters. 

Frustration with Republicans in Kean’s Democratic-leaning hometown 

Westfield, Kean’s hometown, a New York City suburb, leans Democratic. In the 2024 election, former Vice President Kamala Harris won in the town and Kean lost to his Democratic opponent by around 3,000 votes – although he won the district overall. 

Lena Rella, a registered Democrat, said she isn’t sure if she’ll vote in this election because she’s burnt out by politics, but would probably vote against Kean just because he’s a Republican. 

Still, Rella noted that she voted for Kean in 2022 over then-Rep. Tom Malinowski, a Democrat. “It was his legacy, his father, and what he did,” she said before going on to say that she supported Kean as a fellow Westfield resident. 

Rella said that his personal struggles and absence don’t really play a part and that she thinks “it was great that he said what he went through” and that “if he didn't then there might have been some confusion.” 

“I can't even imagine. Me and my husband talk about it sometimes because now all the commercials,” she said. “He must have been not feeling too good for him to be out that long.” 

Another Westfield resident, Ingrid McKinley, said she’s voting for Bennett in November, saying that Kean’s voting has been too aligned with the Trump administration for her preferences. 

Robert Algarin shared that he has met Kean a few times at fundraisers and community barbecues and "he's not a bad man" but, in his opinion, “Republicans have dropped the ball on the institutional integrity of what they're supposed to be doing in Congress.” 

Algarin was previously a registered Republican but switched his party affiliation to independent, explaining that because of the Trump administration, he will vote Democrat. 

He also explained that he does not support any member from either party taking prolonged absences, highlighting Kean and Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Kentucky, as examples of people who “have a job they just don't show up to for a couple of months.” 

“They get paid. That's wrong. That's not just him. The Democrats do the same thing, but that's got to change,” Algarin said. “Unfortunately, the Republicans are doing that more right now, not showing up to work and getting paid for it.”
